topics.title: Exit plan (leaving the island)
topics.short: The "Leave the island" view: can you leave, when, how, and what to do first. It checks waves, wind, TMD sea warnings, cyclones and heavy rain, and lists the routes.
topics.body:
Samui can only be left by sea (car ferries, passenger boats, catamarans) or by air. The exit plan gathers:

- Signals now: waves, TMD Gulf sea warnings, wind gusts, tropical cyclones, heavy rain. Each is ok, caution, blocked or unknown.
- Departure windows for the next 7 days (see Departure windows).
- Routes: Seatran and Raja car ferries to Donsak, Lomprayah boats to Donsak or Chumphon, flights from Samui (USM) or Surat Thani (URT), trains from Surat Thani. Only official operator sites are linked; no schedules or prices (they change).
- Checklist before leaving: documents, cash, medicine, confirming the crossing, telling someone, charged phone, go-bag, and securing the house.

Missing or stale data shows as unknown, never ok.
topics.why_it_matters: Leave early, while ferries and flights still run. When the sea closes, everyone tries to fly out at once and seats run out.

rows: within 300 km, or orange/red within 800 km
TMD heavy-rain bulletin or 90 mm/24 h forecast

sources.title: Thai DDPM -- Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (hotline 1784)

topics.title: Exit routes: ferries
topics.short: Boats from Samui to the mainland.
topics.body:
Car and passenger ferries: Seatran Ferry (Nathon to Donsak) and Raja Ferry (Lipa Noi to Donsak). Lomprayah: boat + bus to Donsak / Surat Thani, and high-speed catamaran to Chumphon via Koh Phangan and Koh Tao.

Limits. No schedules or fares are given: they change. Only official websites that answered on 2026-09-24 are linked.
topics.how_to_read: Check the day's departures and cancellations on the operator's site or at the pier. Car ferries are the most weather-resistant; the Chumphon catamaran is the most exposed.
topics.why_it_matters: Ferries carry most people, vehicles and pets off the island and stop first in rough seas.

topics.title: Exit routes: flights
topics.short: Flights from Samui airport (USM) and from Surat Thani airport (URT) on the mainland.
topics.body:
Samui International Airport (most flights by Bangkok Airways; Thai Airways also sells Bangkok-Samui). Surat Thani airport, reached after the ferry, has more airlines and seats (e.g. Nok Air, AirAsia).

Limits. No schedules or fares are given. Pets and large luggage have airline-specific rules.
topics.how_to_read: Check seats and flight status on the airline sites the same day. Bangkok Airways' site blocks automated checks, so open it in a browser.
topics.why_it_matters: The airport stays open when ferries stop for waves, but seats are few and expensive when everyone leaves; storms can close it too.

topics.title: Exit routes: train from Surat Thani
topics.short: Trains from Surat Thani station (Phun Phin) on the mainland.
topics.body:
The State Railway of Thailand's southern line links Surat Thani with Bangkok and the rest of the network; tickets are sold online (D-Ticket).

Limits. Floods in the South can cut the line during the northeast monsoon; check before relying on it.
topics.how_to_read: Useful after the ferry when flights are full. Check the train and seats on the SRT sites.
topics.why_it_matters: A high-capacity onward option once you are on the mainland.

topics.title: Exit signal: heavy rain
topics.short: Forecast heavy rain and TMD heavy-rain bulletins for the South.
topics.body:
Maximum daily rain forecast for Samui (today + 2 days) and any TMD heavy-rain bulletin in force for the South / Gulf.

Limits. Rain forecasts are uncertain at this scale; a TMD bulletin covers a large area, not only Samui.
topics.how_to_read: A TMD bulletin or 90 mm or more in a day: caution (flooded roads to the piers and on the mainland). 150 mm or more: blocked.
topics.why_it_matters: Leaving by ferry means driving to the pier and on through Surat Thani, where roads and the railway can flood in the monsoon.

topics.title: Exit signal: TMD sea warnings
topics.short: Thai Meteorological Department warning bulletins about waves in the Gulf of Thailand.
topics.body:
The app reads TMD bulletins, keeps those in force for the South / Gulf and checks for wave warnings and the advice that small boats should stay ashore.

Limits. Bulletins are in Thai and summarised; the app detects keywords, so read the bulletin itself when it matters.
topics.how_to_read: No Gulf wave warning: ok. Wave warning for the Gulf: caution. 'Small boats should stay ashore' or waves of 3 m or more: blocked. Andaman-Sea-only warnings do not count.
topics.why_it_matters: The TMD is the official source that ferry operators and the port authorities follow.

topics.title: Exit signal: tropical cyclone nearby
topics.short: The nearest tropical cyclone reported by GDACS or NASA EONET.
topics.body:
Distance from home to each active cyclone's last reported position.

Limits. The last reported position is used, not the forecast track. Check the TMD for the official track.
topics.how_to_read: None within 800 km: ok. Any cyclone within 800 km: caution. Within 300 km, or an orange/red GDACS alert within 800 km: blocked. Feeds not received recently: unknown. A cyclone signal also marks the first 3 days of the departure windows.
topics.why_it_matters: Cyclones reach Samui rarely but hard (Harriet 1962, Gay 1989, Pabuk 2019), mostly October-January. The sea closes before the storm arrives, so the time to leave is while it is still far away.

topics.title: Exit signal: waves
topics.short: Forecast maximum wave height off Samui, today and the next 2 days.
topics.body:
Daily maximum significant wave height from the Open-Meteo marine model, for open water east of the island.

Limits. A model value for one grid point; the Donsak ferries cross the more sheltered southwest side, the Chumphon catamaran the open Gulf. Operators decide cancellations themselves.
topics.how_to_read: Below 2 m: ok. 2 to 3 m: caution (catamarans and small boats are cancelled first). 3 m or more: blocked (car ferries likely suspended). No recent forecast: unknown.
topics.why_it_matters: The ferries to Donsak and the catamarans to Chumphon are the main way off the island.

topics.title: Exit signal: wind gusts
topics.short: Forecast maximum wind gusts on Samui, today and the next 2 days.
topics.body:
Daily maximum gust from the Open-Meteo forecast (km/h).

Limits. Gusts are model values; squalls in thunderstorms can be stronger and are not forecast precisely.
topics.how_to_read: Below 62 km/h: ok (gusts of 45-60 km/h are routine in the monsoons). 62 to 75 km/h (gale, Beaufort 8): caution. 75 km/h or more (strong gale, Beaufort 9): blocked.
topics.why_it_matters: Strong wind builds the sea quickly and can also close the airport.

topics.title: Factor: air quality (PM2.5, haze)
topics.short: The worse of the last 24-hour average of PM2.5 and the worst 24-hour average forecast for the next 72 hours, scored with the Thai PCD bands.
topics.body: Data: modelled PM2.5 from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), through Open-Meteo. It is a model, not a monitoring station: compare with Air4Thai (the Thai Pollution Control Department network) when in doubt.
topics.why_it_matters: Samui is usually clean, but El Nino years bring haze from fires in Indonesia and Malaysia (2015, 2019).

thresholds.note: Cap: 3. Not a critical factor. Stale after 12 h without an update.

related.title: AQI (air quality index): Thai vs US

sources.title: Air4Thai -- Thai Pollution Control Department air quality
Thailand.go.th -- Thailand adjusts AQI criteria for PM2.5 (2023)

topics.title: Factor: El Nino (event strength)
topics.short: Scores how strong El Nino is, from the latest ONI and weekly Nino 3.4. It can raise the overall level to Prepare but never higher: it is a warning sign, not a direct threat.
topics.body:
The factor takes the higher of two levels: one from the latest ONI and one from the latest weekly Nino 3.4 anomaly. The explanation also shows the NOAA alert status and the highest El Nino probability in the IRI forecast (for context; they do not change the level).

It is marked stale if the newest ONI is more than 120 days old.
topics.why_it_matters: A strong El Nino usually means below-normal rain and a hotter, longer dry season in Thailand. For Samui, the water risk window is February-April 2027.

thresholds.note: Cap in the overall level: 2. Critical factor.

related.title: Weak, moderate, strong and "super" El Nino
How the overall level is decided (rules R1-R4)

sources.title: NOAA CPC -- Oceanic Nino Index table (ERSSTv6)

topics.title: Factor: extreme heat
topics.short: Uses the highest forecast feels-like temperature over the next 7 days, and how many days reach 41 °C, plus how much warmer than normal the last 30 days were.
topics.body:
Main measure: the maximum daily feels-like (apparent) temperature forecast for the next 7 days (Open-Meteo), and the number of days at 41 °C or more.

It can also be raised by a persistent warm spell: if the daily maximum temperature over the last 30 days (ERA5) averaged 1.5 °C above normal, at least 1; 2.5 °C above normal, at least 2.

Why start at 39 °C: on Samui a feels-like of 32-38 °C is an ordinary day, so the thresholds are set higher than the "caution" bands.
topics.why_it_matters: Above 41 °C feels-like, heatstroke is possible, especially for children, older people and during exertion. Power cuts (no air conditioning) make it worse. El Nino makes March-May 2027 likely hotter than normal.

thresholds.note: Cap in the overall level: 3. Critical factor. Stale after 36 h without a forecast update. Heat >= 3 together with water >= 3 sets the overall level to 4 (rule R4b).

related.title: How the overall level is decided (rules R1-R4)

sources.title: US National Weather Service -- Heat index

topics.title: Factor: heavy rain / flooding
topics.short: Uses the 3-day rain forecast (biggest day and 72-hour total), island rain gauges, TMD heavy-rain warnings and how wet the ground already is.
topics.body:
Main measure: the largest 24-hour rain and the 72-hour total in the Open-Meteo forecast for the next 3 days. A fresh island rain gauge reading (less than 6 hours old) is also scored with the 24-hour column.

Raised when:

- A TMD heavy-rain warning for the area is in force: at least 1.
- The past 7 days already brought 150 mm or more and the level is 1 or 2: +1 level (the same rain on saturated ground floods and slides more).
- The past 7 days brought 250 mm or more: at least 1, even without more rain forecast (landslides, slow drainage).
topics.why_it_matters: October-December (northeast monsoon) brings Samui's heaviest rain and floods, even in an El Nino year. Coastal roads and the Lamai/Chaweng area can flood; landslides are possible on slopes.

thresholds.note: Rain classes from the TMD (see Rain amount classes). Cap: 3. Critical factor.

sources.title: Thai Meteorological Department -- weather criteria (rain amounts, hot weather, in Thai)

topics.title: Factor: marine heat / coral bleaching
topics.short: NOAA Coral Reef Watch Degree Heating Weeks for the Gulf of Thailand stations. Context only: it can raise the overall level to Watch at most.
topics.body: Uses the latest DHW of the Coral Reef Watch stations, preferring those around Samui and the Gulf of Thailand. Stale if the newest value is more than 10 days old.

thresholds.note: Cap: 1. Not a critical factor.

sources.title: NOAA Coral Reef Watch -- Degree Heating Week
NOAA Coral Reef Watch -- Bleaching Alert Area (alert levels)

topics.title: Factor: media and social signal
topics.short: Counts news and social posts from the last 14 days that mention water shortage or flooding on Samui or in Thailand. Low weight, never a trigger on its own.
topics.body:
A simple keyword count (English, French and Thai words for water shortage, drought, flood, landslide) over the app's news and social feeds.

It is deliberately weak: keyword counts can be fooled by old stories, rumours or articles about somewhere else. So it can only add Watch, and only when another factor is already at 1 or more (rule R2). Its main job: point you to local reports worth reading.

rows: fewer than 3 about Samui and fewer than 10 about Thailand
3 or more about Samui, or 10 or more about Thailand
thresholds.note: Cap: 1. Also: 2 or more reports of water shortage on Samui can confirm a water level 4 when rain is already at level 3.

related.title: How the overall level is decided (rules R1-R4)

topics.title: Factor: rain deficit / water shortage
topics.short: Compares rain over the last 90 days (180 days in the dry season) with the 1991-2020 normal, and adds PWA notices, the seasonal forecast, the regional dam and the El Nino season.
topics.body:
Main measure: rain observed (ERA5) over the last 90 days as a % of the 1991-2020 normal for the same days. In the dry season (January-May) the 180-day window drives the level when it is worse, because it holds the last monsoon refill.

Then, raise the level (never lower it) when:

- 60-day rain is below 50% of normal, or 180-day rain below 75%: at least 1.
- October-December (refill season) + strong El Nino (ENSO factor 2) + 90-day rain below 75%: at least 2.
- January-May + strong El Nino: at least 1, or 2 if rain is below 75% of normal.
- ECMWF seasonal forecast below 80% of normal for the next 3 months: at least 1.
- Ratchaprapa dam (mainland, a regional indicator only) below 40%: at least 1; below 25%: at least 2.
- A PWA Samui water-supply notice in force: at least 1; a notice lasting more than 48 h, or "no supply": at least 2.

Safeguards:

- A rain-only level 3 needs at least 100 mm missing in absolute terms; otherwise it stays at 2 (40% of a tiny dry-season normal is not an emergency by itself).
- Level 4 only when a shortage is confirmed: level 3 AND (at least 2 news reports of water shortage on Samui in 14 days, or a long PWA notice).

Not tracked automatically (no machine-readable source): the island reservoir levels and the PWA rotation schedule.
topics.why_it_matters: October-December is when Samui's reservoirs refill (about half of the year's rain). A deficit now is the strongest warning for the 2027 dry season.

columns: Rain, % of 1991-2020 normal (90 d; 180 d in the dry season)
rows: below 40% and at least 100 mm short
level 3 + shortage confirmed on the island
4 (counts as 3 in the overall level, 4 only through rule R4b)
thresholds.note: Cap in the overall level: 3. Critical factor. Stale if ERA5 has not updated for 3 days or the last ERA5 day is more than 10 days old.

sources.title: Bangkok Post, 29/07/2026 -- Koh Samui faces water rationing

topics.title: Factor: sea state (ferries, isolation)
topics.short: The highest forecast wave height near Samui over 72 hours, plus TMD Gulf wave warnings. High seas stop ferries and cut the island off.
topics.body:
Main measure: the maximum significant wave height forecast for the next 72 hours (Open-Meteo Marine). A TMD high-wave warning for the Gulf raises it to at least 1. Andaman-only warnings are ignored: they do not concern Samui.

If the wave forecast is missing but a TMD rough-sea warning is in force, the factor shows 1 Watch.
topics.why_it_matters: Above 2 m, small boats stay in port and ferries may be cancelled: the island is then cut off (supplies, evacuation, water by barge). Only the airport remains, with limited capacity.

rows: 2 to 3 m (small boats stay in port)
thresholds.note: Cap: 3. Critical factor. Stale after 24 h without a marine forecast update.

topics.title: Factor: tropical cyclone / wind
topics.short: Looks for GDACS tropical cyclones by distance to Samui and by alert colour, plus forecast wind gusts for 72 h and TMD storm warnings.
topics.body:
The factor takes the highest of:

- The cyclone level (table below), from GDACS cyclone positions and colours.
- The gust level, from the strongest forecast gust in the next 72 hours (Beaufort scale; Samui often sees 55-70 km/h gusts in the monsoons, so it starts at strong gale).
- A TMD storm warning in force: at least 2.

If neither GDACS nor the TMD has answered recently, the factor is unknown: a cyclone cannot be ruled out.
topics.why_it_matters: Cyclones are rare on Samui but destructive (Harriet 1962, Gay 1989, Pabuk January 2019). They mostly arrive from October to January.

thresholds.note: Cap: 3, except the orange/red cyclone within 300 km, which sets the overall level to 4. Critical factor.

related.title: How the overall level is decided (rules R1-R4)

sources.title: GDACS -- tropical cyclone impact model and alert levels

topics.title: Fakes: how to spot official stores
topics.short: Masks, water filters, power banks and branded batteries are often faked. On Lazada buy from LazMall stores, on Shopee from Shopee Mall stores (official brand shops), or from a big retailer.
topics.body:
Warning signs of a fake or unsafe product:

- A price far below the other listings (for example a famous-brand filter or mask at a fraction of the usual price).
- A seller that is not the brand's official shop, with few ratings.
- Missing certification marks (N95 / KN95 / P2 on masks; the Thai TIS mark on power banks) or blurry printing.
- A power bank that is much lighter than a genuine one of the same capacity.

Safer choices:

- LazMall (Lazada) and Shopee Mall (Shopee) list official brand stores and authorised sellers.
- Big retailers (Makro, HomePro, Global House, Boots) sell through their own shops.
- Keep the receipt, check the product on arrival, and test power banks and radios before you need them.
topics.why_it_matters: A fake mask does not filter haze, a fake filter can let bacteria through and a fake power bank can overheat. In an emergency you only find out when it is too late.

topics.title: Feels-like temperature and heat index
topics.short: How hot it feels to the body, combining air temperature with humidity (and in some formulas wind and sun). In humid Samui it is often several degrees above the air temperature.
topics.body:
Sweat cools you by evaporating. In humid air it evaporates slowly, so you feel hotter than the thermometer says. The "heat index" (US National Weather Service) and the "apparent temperature" (the Open-Meteo value used here, which also accounts for wind and solar radiation) both try to express this.

Heat index values assume shade. Full sunshine can add up to 8 °C (15 °F) according to the NWS.

Thai health and weather agencies use four heat index bands adapted from the NWS (table). The current NWS chart uses slightly lower upper bands (danger from 39.4 °C / 103 °F, extreme danger from 51.7 °C / 125 °F). This app's heat factor uses its own thresholds of 39, 41 and 54 °C (see Factor: extreme heat).
topics.why_it_matters: Heat is the most common El Nino hazard for people in Thailand. The risk is highest in March-May, during exertion, for older people and children, and during power cuts.

rows: Fatigue with prolonged exposure or activity
Heat cramps, heat exhaustion or heat stroke possible with prolonged exposure or activity
Heat cramps or exhaustion likely; heat stroke possible

sources.title: US National Weather Service -- Heat index

topics.title: Fire detections (NASA FIRMS)
topics.short: Hot spots detected by satellites in the last 24 hours, mostly vegetation fires and burning. Many fires in Sumatra, Borneo or mainland Southeast Asia can mean haze.
topics.body:
NASA FIRMS lists places where satellite sensors (VIIRS and MODIS) saw something much hotter than its surroundings during an overpass. Most are fires: forest and peat fires, crop burning.

Limits: a satellite only sees a place a few times a day; clouds and smoke hide fires; small fires can be missed; some hot spots are industrial sites. One dot is not one fire.
topics.how_to_read: Clusters of dots matter more than single ones. Fires far away only affect Samui if the winds carry the smoke towards the Gulf of Thailand.
topics.why_it_matters: In El Nino years, peat and forest fires in Indonesia and Malaysia can send haze across the region (2015, 2019). Crop burning on the mainland peaks in the dry season.

sources.title: NASA FIRMS -- Fire Information for Resource Management System

topics.title: Flood (heavy rain, river, coast)
topics.short: The worst of three parts: days with 50 mm of rain or more, the height of the place above the nearest large river (GloFAS), and low-lying coast.
topics.body:
- Heavy rain: ERA5 days per year with >= 50 mm. ERA5 is a ~30 km model and smooths peaks: real local downpours are stronger.
- River: the largest river cell (mean flow >= 1 m3/s) within about 15 km, from GloFAS. What matters is how far the place sits above it: a hilltop village above an estuary is not exposed to river floods.
- Coast: when a sea cell is within 10 km and the place is low (elevation from the Copernicus DEM).

See River discharge (GloFAS) for the river forecast.
topics.why_it_matters: Floods damage homes, cut roads and ferries, and contaminate water. Check the exact plot before buying or renting.

thresholds.note: Score = the highest part. Elevations are at the place point: individual streets can be lower. Exposure scale: 0 very low, 1 low, 2 moderate, 3 high, 4 very high. Higher = more exposed. The colour of the matrix cell follows the same scale.

topics.title: Flood water (VIIRS 3-day)
topics.short: Land under water that is not normally flooded, last 3 days.
topics.body:
NASA LANCE flood product from the VIIRS instruments on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21.

Limits. Clouds hide floods; no red does not prove no flooding. 375 m pixels miss small floods.
topics.how_to_read: Red = flood, yellow = recurring seasonal flood, light blue = normal water, grey = not enough clear views (clouds).
topics.why_it_matters: Monsoon floods in southern Thailand (Nakhon Si Thammarat, Surat Thani) cut roads and ferries' feeder routes.

topics.title: Forecast uncertainty and the spring barrier
topics.short: ENSO forecasts made in the northern spring (March-May) are much less reliable. From mid-year, forecasts for the coming winter peak become quite skilful.
topics.body:
ENSO forecasts have a weak spot every year, called the spring predictability barrier. Forecasts that cross the northern spring (March to May) are much less accurate.

Why (NOAA Climate.gov):

- Spring is a transition time: events decay after their winter peak, pass through neutral, or start to form.
- The ocean and atmosphere are only weakly coupled then, because the temperature contrasts across the Pacific are smallest.
- In short: the signal is small and the noise is large.

After spring, skill improves. Using July-August data, models predict about three-quarters of the winter ENSO ups and downs.

Rules of thumb:

- A forecast made in September for December is fairly reliable.
- A forecast for next May to July is much less reliable, whoever makes it.
- Forecasts of local impacts (rain on Samui) are less certain than forecasts of Nino 3.4.
topics.why_it_matters: Forecasts for how the 2026 El Nino peaks around the end of 2026 are fairly solid now. Forecasts for when it ends in mid-2027 will stay uncertain until spring 2027.

sources.title: NOAA Climate.gov -- The spring predictability barrier

topics.title: Freshness ("as of" dates)
topics.short: Every value carries the date of the data itself (not of the download) and a link to its source. Each source has a maximum age matching how often it really updates.
topics.body:
Different data arrive at very different speeds:

- Disaster alerts (GDACS): every few minutes.
- Weather forecasts (Open-Meteo): several times a day.
- Weekly Nino SST (NOAA CPC): once a week.
- Satellite images: daily, one or more days behind.
- ERA5 observed rain for Samui: about 5 days behind.
- Monthly indices (ONI, RONI, SOI, MEI): once a month, and a 3-month mean is centred on a month that ended weeks ago.

So "as of 2026-07-15" on the ONI is normal (that is the centre of June-August), while "as of" two weeks ago on a weather forecast is a problem. The app compares each value with its source's maximum age and marks it stale when it is too old.

topics.title: GDACS alerts (green, orange, red)
topics.short: A UN / European Commission system that rates each new disaster by its likely humanitarian impact: green (low), orange (medium), red (high, international help likely needed).
topics.body:
GDACS (Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System) is run by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre with the UN. It automatically detects cyclones, floods, droughts, earthquakes, volcanoes and wildfires, and estimates their impact.

The colour is about impact on people, not only about the strength of the hazard. It combines hazard severity, how many people are exposed, and how vulnerable the country is. For tropical cyclones, for example:

- Green: for example a tropical storm affecting fewer than 10 million people, or storm surge up to 1 m.
- Orange: for example a Category 1-2 cyclone affecting 100,000+ people in medium-to-high vulnerability areas, or surge of 1-3 m.
- Red: for example a Category 3 cyclone affecting 100,000+ people in medium-to-high vulnerability areas, or surge of 3 m or more.

A strong storm over an empty ocean can be green. The alert is automatic and can change as the storm moves.
topics.how_to_read: Coloured symbols on the Map. Click one for the GDACS report link. Distance to Samui matters as much as the colour.
topics.why_it_matters: The cyclone part of the Samui risk level uses GDACS: an orange or red tropical cyclone within 300 km of Samui is the only single hazard that sets the level to 4 Leave (rule R4a).

topics.title: GISTEMP global and tropical anomaly
topics.short: gistemp_global_anom (monthly) and gistemp_tropics_annual_anom (yearly, 24S-24N).
topics.body:
NASA GISS temperature departures from 1951-1980, global monthly and tropical yearly.

Limits. The yearly tropical value only appears once the year is complete.
topics.how_to_read: degC above normal. Dated the 15th of the month (monthly) or 1 July (yearly).
topics.why_it_matters: Shows the global heat that El Nino adds on top of long-term warming.

topics.title: Global air temperature, daily (ERA5)
topics.short: era5_global_t2m and era5_global_t2m_anom.
topics.body:
Daily global mean air temperature at 2 m from Copernicus Climate Pulse, and its difference from 1991-2020.

Limits. Last 2-3 days preliminary (meta.status).
topics.how_to_read: degC. The anomaly is what matters: around +0.8 in September 2026.
topics.why_it_matters: The planet usually sets new daily records a few months after a strong El Nino peaks.

topics.title: Global sea surface temperature, daily (ERA5, 60S-60N)
topics.short: era5_sst_6060 and era5_sst_6060_anom.
topics.body:
Daily mean sea surface temperature between 60S and 60N from Copernicus Climate Pulse, and its difference from 1991-2020.

Limits. Last 2-3 days preliminary. Not the same dataset as the OISST world SST series.
topics.how_to_read: degC; around 21.0 degC and +0.7 in late September 2026.
topics.why_it_matters: Ocean heat drives air temperature and coral bleaching risk; El Nino raises it.

topics.title: Global temperature (climate context)
topics.short: How warm the whole planet and its oceans are compared with normal, from four agencies. It is background: El Nino adds to it for a few months.
topics.body:
This group gathers the global temperature records:

- ERA5 (Copernicus Climate Pulse): daily global air temperature at 2 m and daily sea surface temperature between 60 S and 60 N, with anomalies from 1991-2020 (Global air temperature, daily (ERA5), Global sea surface temperature, daily (ERA5, 60S-60N)).
- Met Office HadCRUT5 / HadSST4: monthly global land + sea, global sea and tropical sea anomalies, from 1961-1990 (Met Office global and tropical anomalies).
- NASA GISTEMP: monthly global and yearly tropical anomalies, from 1951-1980 (GISTEMP global and tropical anomaly).
- NOAA NCEI: monthly global and Asian land anomalies, from 1901-2000 (NOAA global and Asia monthly anomalies).
topics.how_to_read:
- Values are anomalies in °C: the difference from each agency's own baseline period. An older baseline gives a bigger number for the same year, so compare the shapes of the lines, not the values across agencies.
- Daily ERA5 values arrive 2-3 days late; the monthly records about 1-6 weeks after the month ends.
topics.why_it_matters: A strong El Nino usually lifts the global mean by roughly 0.1-0.2 °C a few months after its peak, on top of the long warming trend. It explains why records can fall in 2027 and why the sea around Samui runs warm (coral bleaching risk).

topics.title: GRACE-FO drought maps for Asia
topics.short: Latest weekly groundwater and soil-moisture drought maps (images).
topics.body:
Status key grace_drought_asia {date, maps: [{id: gws|rtzsm|sfsm, title, url, pdf}], legend}.

Limits. Coarse (~300 km underlying resolution); weekly.
topics.how_to_read: Wetness percentile vs 1948-2012: dark red <= 2, red 2-5, orange 5-10, tan 10-20, yellow 20-30, white 30-70 normal, blues wetter.
topics.why_it_matters: Shows long-lasting El Nino drought in Thailand's groundwater and soils.

topics.title: Heat stress (days with feels-like above 35 °C)
topics.short: How many days a year the feels-like maximum exceeds 35 °C (ERA5, 1991-2020 average). Humid tropical places score high even when the air temperature looks moderate.
topics.body: Counted from ERA5 daily feels-like (apparent) maximum temperature, averaged over 1991-2020. Feels-like uses temperature, humidity and wind, so humid heat counts more than dry heat.
topics.why_it_matters: Heat stress affects sleep, health (especially for older people and children), work and electricity bills for air conditioning. El Nino years add heat in Southeast Asia.

thresholds.note: Exposure scale: 0 very low, 1 low, 2 moderate, 3 high, 4 very high. Higher = more exposed. The colour of the matrix cell follows the same scale.

sources.title: US National Weather Service -- Heat index

topics.title: History loading state ("loading, not estimated")
topics.short: The ERA5 history is fetched in decade windows, one per hour after start-up. Until every window is stored, the numbers that need a missing month are blank and labelled "loading, not estimated".
topics.how_to_read: A green "complete" state with a recent ERA5 date is the normal case. "Loading" with a list of windows means come back later, or check the Sources page (source samui_era5_history).
topics.why_it_matters: A blank cell is a promise: the page would rather show nothing than a number that was not computed from the data.

related.title: Analogs: the numbers behind each event
The Sources page and source states

topics.title: Hotspot counts (ASMC)
topics.short: The daily number of fire hotspots per country or region counted by the ASEAN haze centre. A sudden rise, with dry weather, is an early haze warning.
topics.body:
The ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) counts satellite fire hotspots (VIIRS, daytime, high confidence) per region every day. The app charts the last 14 days.

Hotspot counts depend on clouds (fewer seen on cloudy days), so look at the trend over several days, not one day.

sources.title: ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre -- regional haze

topics.title: How the overall level is decided (rules R1-R4)
topics.short: R1: the highest factor wins (after caps). R2: news never triggers alone. R3: two physical hazards at Prepare = Act. R4: Leave only for a close orange/red cyclone or extreme heat plus a water crisis.
topics.body:
The engine combines the factors with four documented rules:

- R1, the highest factor wins. Overall level = the highest factor level, after applying each factor's cap. Caps: El Nino 2; water, heat, flood, cyclone/wind, sea state and air 3; marine heat 1; news 1.
- R2, news never decides alone. The news factor only counts if another factor is at 1 or more.
- R3, combined hazards. If two physical hazards (among water, heat, flood, cyclone/wind, sea state, air) are both at 2 Prepare or more, the overall level is at least 3 Act. Example: heavy rain while 2 m seas stop the ferries.
- R4, Leave (4) only when safety or basic supplies are directly threatened:
  - R4a: an orange or red GDACS tropical cyclone within 300 km of Samui (cyclone/wind factor = 4).
  - R4b: extreme heat (heat >= 3) together with a water supply crisis (water >= 3).

The Samui page lists which rules fired, and "what would raise the level" (the next trigger for each factor).
topics.example: ONI at +1.8 °C gives the El Nino factor 2 (Prepare). All other factors at 0 or 1. Overall = 2 Prepare by R1, even if the weather today is fine.

sources.title: GDACS -- Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System

topics.title: Indian Ocean Dipole (DMI)
topics.short: The temperature difference between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean; positive values usually mean a drier season around Thailand and Indonesia.
topics.body:
The Dipole Mode Index (DMI) is the sea surface temperature anomaly of the west pole (10N-10S, 50E-70E) minus the east pole (0-10S, 90E-110E), monthly, from the Japan Meteorological Agency (1991-2020 base). Series dmi_jma_anom, with iod_west_jma_anom and iod_east_jma_anom for the two poles (degC).

Limits. Monthly values, published about 2 weeks after the month. JMA's analysis can differ by a few tenths from NOAA's or BoM's DMI.
topics.how_to_read: Above about +0.4 C for several months = positive IOD; below -0.4 C = negative IOD; in between = neutral. Positive IOD events usually peak in Sep-Nov and fade by December.
topics.why_it_matters: Southern Thailand and the Maritime Continent get less rain during a positive IOD, and a positive IOD during El Nino adds to the drying. It also changes the haze risk from Sumatra and Borneo fires.

topics.title: IRI ENSO forecast (plume and probabilities)
topics.short: Columbia University's monthly summary of about 20 computer models: for each 3-month season ahead, the chance of El Nino, neutral or La Nina.
topics.body:
The International Research Institute for Climate and Society (IRI) collects forecasts of the Nino 3.4 anomaly from many models (22 in the current release: 13 dynamical and 9 statistical).

- The plume is a chart with one line per model for the next 9 overlapping 3-month seasons. When the lines are close together, the models agree.
- The probabilities turn this into chances for each season: El Nino (+0.5 °C or more), neutral (-0.5 to +0.5 °C), La Nina (-0.5 °C or less). The three add up to 100%.

Seasons are named by their months' initials: SON = September-October-November, DJF = December-January-February, and so on (see Season codes (DJF, JJA, SON...)).
topics.how_to_read: Read the bar for each season: the red part is the El Nino chance. 90% means "9 chances in 10"; it is not a measure of strength. A forecast for 8 months ahead is much less reliable than one for next season (see Forecast uncertainty and the spring barrier).
topics.why_it_matters: It tells you how long El Nino conditions are likely to last. If El Nino is still likely through February-April 2027, Samui's dry season is likely to be affected.
topics.example: IRI September 2026: El Nino probability 100% from SON 2026 through FMA 2027, 99% in MAM 2027, 90% in AMJ 2027, then 61% in MJJ 2027.

related.title: Forecast uncertainty and the spring barrier

topics.title: JMA El Nino outlook (Japan)
topics.short: The Japan Meteorological Agency's monthly ENSO assessment and 6-month outlook. JMA defines El Nino with the Nino 3 region, not Nino 3.4.
topics.body:
JMA's Tokyo Climate Center publishes a monthly El Nino outlook. Its definition differs from NOAA's:

- Region: NINO.3 (5° N-5° S, 150° W-90° W).
- Rule: the 5-month running mean of the NINO.3 SST deviation stays at +0.5 °C or more for 6 consecutive months or longer.
- The deviation is measured from a sliding 30-year normal.

So JMA and NOAA can declare the start or end of an event a month or two apart. That is normal: they use different yardsticks.

sources.title: JMA Tokyo Climate Center -- El Nino monitoring and outlook
JMA -- Monitoring and Prediction of El Nino (definition, PDF)

topics.title: JMA typhoon tracks
topics.short: Every active West Pacific / South China Sea tropical storm from the official WMO regional centre in Tokyo, with its 5-day forecast.
topics.body:
The Japan Meteorological Agency is the WMO Regional Specialized Meteorological Centre for the western North Pacific and the South China Sea. For each active storm we show its past track, forecast positions at 12-120 h, class (TD, TS, STS, TY), winds and the closest forecast approach to Koh Samui.

Limits. Forecast positions have large errors after 3 days (the probability circles grow to 400 km at 5 days). Only storms JMA is tracking are listed; weak lows in the Gulf may never be named.
topics.how_to_read: Severity on the map: red = the track or forecast passes within 300 km of Samui, orange = within the watch radius (800 km), green = further. Winds are 10-minute averages in knots (JMA convention), lower than JTWC's 1-minute winds for the same storm.
topics.why_it_matters: Storms that hit the Gulf of Thailand (Harriet 1962, Gay 1989, Pabuk 2019) come from the South China Sea, mostly October to January. A storm crossing the Philippines toward Vietnam is the one to watch.

topics.title: JTWC tropical cyclone warnings
topics.short: US Joint Typhoon Warning Center warnings for the NW Pacific and North Indian Ocean, plus its daily advisory of developing disturbances.
topics.body:
JTWC issues a warning every 6 hours for each tropical cyclone: position, 1-minute sustained winds and gusts, and a 5-day forecast track. Its Significant Tropical Weather Advisory also lists disturbances that could develop, west to the Malay Peninsula.

Limits. A military forecast centre, not Thailand's official warning service: the TMD's warnings are the official ones for Thailand. JTWC winds (1-minute) are higher than JMA's (10-minute) for the same storm.
topics.how_to_read: Same map severity as the JMA storms (red within 300 km, orange within 800 km). 'Final warning' means the storm is dissipating or has moved out; it is shown in green. Winds are in knots.
topics.why_it_matters: JTWC covers the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea as well as the South China Sea, and its advisory often flags a Gulf of Thailand disturbance before it gets a name.

topics.title: Judging sea state from a beach or pier cam (ferry decisions)
topics.short: Turn what a beach or pier cam shows into a rough wind / wave estimate before a ferry.
topics.body:
A way to turn what you see on a coastal camera into a rough wind / wave estimate, using the Beaufort scale sailors have used for 200 years.

Limits.

- A camera shows the sea near shore. Mid-channel waves can be bigger.
- Lenses flatten waves; a wide angle makes 2 m look like 1 m.
- Night: nothing useful. Use the marine forecast instead.
- This is a sanity check. The official TMD warning and the ferry operator's decision always win.
topics.how_to_read:
Look at open water, not the shore break, and watch for 30-60 seconds:
- Calm to light (Beaufort 0-2, < 7 knots): glassy or small ripples, no white. Ferries run normally.
- Gentle to moderate (Bft 3-4, 7-16 kt, waves ~0.5-1 m): a few scattered whitecaps. Normal crossing, some spray on speedboats.
- Fresh (Bft 5, 17-21 kt, ~2 m): many whitecaps everywhere, some spray. Speedboats and small boats may be cancelled; big car ferries usually run but it is rough.
- Strong (Bft 6-7, 22-33 kt, 3-4 m): large waves with white foam crests, foam blown in streaks, spray. Expect cancellations; do not take a small boat.
- Gale (Bft 8+): sea heaps up, long foam streaks. Boats stay in port. Also check: rain curtains (grey vertical streaks) moving toward the camera = a squall arriving in minutes; a hazy, milky horizon = poor visibility.

Which cams: north coast (Fisherman's Village, Big Buddha / Bangrak) for the Samui to Phangan / Tao crossing; Bang Po (north-west) for the Nathon / Donsak lane; Koh Tao Mae Haad for the far end; east coast (Crystal Bay, Lamai) for NE-monsoon swell.
topics.why_it_matters: Leaving the island means a boat or a Bangkok Airways flight. From about October to December the north-east monsoon brings wind and waves to the Gulf of Thailand; the Thai Meteorological Department then advises small boats to stay ashore when waves reach 2-3 m. El Nino changes how wet and stormy that season is.

topics.title: Koh Samui risk levels (0-4)
topics.short: One overall level for the island, from 0 Normal to 4 Leave, computed from 9 factors with documented rules. Each factor shows its value, threshold and source.
topics.body:
The Samui page turns many numbers into one answer: how worried should you be, and what should you do now?

How it works, in short:

- 9 factors are scored from 0 to 4 each: El Nino, water, heat, flood, cyclone/wind, sea state, air quality, marine heat and news. See The 9 risk factors.
- 4 rules combine them into one overall level. See How the overall level is decided (rules R1-R4).
- If a critical factor has no current data, the level becomes Unknown, never "Normal". See Data coverage.

Every factor shows its value, the threshold that applies, the explanation, the source and the time of the data. Nothing is hidden in a black-box score.
topics.why_it_matters: The level is a planning aid, not an official warning. When Thai authorities (TMD, DDPM, the province) issue orders, follow them first.

rows: Nothing abnormal expected on the island.
Keep a basic 3-day stock; review the Preparedness page once a month.
Something is building up somewhere (El Nino, a rain deficit, a distant storm).
Check the page daily, follow TMD warnings, build 7 days of drinking water, note ferry and airport contacts.
A real hazard is likely in the coming days or season.
Build 14 days of self-sufficiency, fill the cistern, charge batteries, copy documents, decide your departure threshold.
A hazard is here or imminent, or two hazards combine.
Apply the matching scenario, stock water and fuel, pack the go-bag, check ferries and flights every morning.
Safety or basic supplies are directly threatened.
Leave while ferries and flights run, or follow the authorities (DDPM 1784).
thresholds.note: Full action lists are on the Learn page ("What to do at each level") and on the Samui page. The engine calls level 1 "vigilance" internally; it is shown as Watch.

topics.title: Koh Samui's seasons
topics.short: Samui (Gulf side) gets its main rain from the northeast monsoon, October to January, wettest around November. The dry, hot season runs February to May. The southwest monsoon (June-September) is mild on Samui.
topics.body:
Samui's calendar is the reverse of Phuket's and most of Thailand's, because it sits on the Gulf of Thailand side, sheltered from the southwest monsoon:

- October to January, northeast monsoon: the real rainy season. The ERA5 1991-2020 normal at Samui gives about 282 mm in October, 284 mm in November and 148 mm in December: close to half of the roughly 1,530 mm year falls in October-December. Floods, rough seas in the Gulf and the rare cyclones come in this period. It is also when reservoirs refill.
- February to May, dry and hot season: February is the driest month (about 39 mm). March to May is the heat peak. Water stored during the monsoon is used up.
- June to September, southwest monsoon: Samui is relatively sheltered; rain is moderate. Andaman-side storms and wave warnings mostly do not apply.

The TMD monthly summaries describe the same pattern: heavy to very heavy rain on the east coast of the South in November-December under the northeast monsoon.
topics.why_it_matters: With El Nino, the danger window for water is February-April 2027, and for heat March-May. The flood and sea risk is highest now, October-January, El Nino or not.

topics.title: La Nina
topics.short: The cool phase of ENSO: the central and eastern tropical Pacific is cooler than normal and the trade winds are stronger. For Thailand it tends to mean more rain.
topics.body:
La Nina is the opposite of El Nino. The central and eastern tropical Pacific is cooler than normal, the trade winds blow harder, and the warm water and rain clouds are pushed even further west, over Indonesia and Southeast Asia.

La Nina often follows a strong El Nino, but not always. It typically lasts 1 to 3 years, longer than a typical El Nino (9 to 12 months).
topics.how_to_read: La Nina conditions: one-month relative Nino 3.4 anomaly of -0.5 °C or less, with the 3-month RONI expected to stay below -0.5 °C, plus an atmospheric response.
topics.why_it_matters: La Nina years tend to be wetter than normal in Thailand. Samui is now in an El Nino, so La Nina matters mostly as the possible next phase in 2027-2028.

sources.title: NOAA CPC -- ENSO frequently asked questions
NOAA CPC -- ENSO Alert System definitions

topics.title: Land surface temperature (8-day)
topics.short: Daytime ground temperature averaged over 8 days.
topics.body:
MODIS Terra 8-day land surface temperature.

Limits. Ground skin temperature, hotter than air in the sun; about 10 days behind.
topics.how_to_read: Kelvin: 300 K = 27 degC, 310 K = 37 degC, 320 K = 47 degC.
topics.why_it_matters: Shows heat building over Thai farmland and towns with fewer cloud gaps than daily data.

topics.title: Land surface temperature (night)
topics.short: Night-time ground temperature.
topics.body:
MODIS Terra night pass (about 10:30 pm).

Limits. Gaps where clouds cover the ground.
topics.how_to_read: Kelvin: 295 K = 22 degC, 300 K = 27 degC.
topics.why_it_matters: Warm nights make heat waves dangerous for health.

topics.title: Layer: aerosols / smoke (optical depth)
topics.short: How much sunlight is blocked by particles (smoke, dust, pollution) in the whole air column. Below 0.1 = clear; about 1 = very hazy; above 2-3 = very high concentrations.
topics.body:
Aerosol optical depth (AOD) is a number without units that measures how much the particles in the air dim the sunlight. NASA's guide: less than 0.1 is a crystal clear sky; a value of 1 means very hazy; above 2 or 3 means very high concentrations.

AOD is for the whole column of air, from the ground to the top of the atmosphere. A thick smoke layer high up can give a high AOD while the air you breathe is fine, and the reverse. For what you breathe, use PM2.5 (see PM2.5 and the Thai bands).
topics.how_to_read: Yellow/orange/red-brown patches (see legend) = more particles. Look for plumes spreading from fire areas in Sumatra and Borneo towards the Malay Peninsula.

sources.title: NASA Earth Observatory -- Aerosol optical depth map guide

topics.title: Layer: chlorophyll (PACE)
topics.short: Satellite estimate of chlorophyll in the sea surface, a sign of plankton. El Nino cuts the cold, nutrient-rich upwelling off Peru, so chlorophyll drops there.
topics.body:
Phytoplankton are microscopic plants that colour the water green. More chlorophyll = more plankton = more food for fish.

Off Peru, cold deep water normally rises to the surface and fertilises the sea. During El Nino the Thermocline deepens, that upwelling weakens, and the plankton (and the fishery) collapses.
topics.how_to_read: Blue/purple = low chlorophyll (clear, poor water); green/yellow/red = high chlorophyll. Clouds leave gaps.

topics.title: Layer: infrared clouds (Himawari)
topics.short: The latest infrared image from Japan's Himawari satellite (updated about every 10 minutes). Bright, cold cloud tops = tall storm clouds; day and night.
topics.body:
Himawari is a geostationary satellite: it stays above the same point over the equator and photographs Asia and the western Pacific every 10 minutes. The infrared channel (band 13) measures the temperature of whatever it sees: the ground, the sea, or cloud tops.

High clouds are very cold, so they stand out. Tall thunderstorms and cyclones have the coldest tops.
topics.how_to_read: The coldest (highest) cloud tops appear brightest or in the strongest colours of the legend; warm ground and sea appear dark. A tight, round mass of cold cloud with spiral bands is a tropical cyclone.

topics.title: Layer: land surface temperature
topics.short: How hot the ground itself is during the day (Terra MODIS), not the air. On a sunny day the ground is often much hotter than the air.
topics.body: Land surface temperature is the temperature of the ground surface (soil, roofs, roads, leaves) seen by a satellite. It is not the air temperature from a weather forecast, and it is not the feels-like temperature. It is useful to spot heatwaves and very dry areas. Clouds hide the ground, so cloudy areas are empty.
topics.how_to_read: Warmer colours = hotter ground (see legend). Compare regions and dates rather than reading exact numbers.

topics.title: Layer: rain (GPM IMERG)
topics.short: Satellite estimate of rain intensity (NASA GPM IMERG). Shows where it is raining hard, even over the ocean where there are no rain gauges.
topics.body: IMERG merges microwave and infrared data from a constellation of satellites, calibrated with rain gauges, into a global rain map. It is an estimate: it can miss short, small showers and can be off over mountains and small islands.
topics.how_to_read: Colours show rain rate (see the legend): light colours = light rain, bright/dark colours = heavy rain. Empty = no rain detected.
topics.why_it_matters: During El Nino, heavy rain shifts to the central Pacific and Southeast Asia gets less. In the northeast monsoon, look for rain bands over the southern Gulf of Thailand.

topics.title: Layer: rain radar (RainViewer)
topics.short: The latest rain radar picture (about every 10 minutes), from national radar networks shared through RainViewer. Shows where it is raining right now.
topics.body:
Weather radars send out pulses and measure the echo from raindrops. RainViewer combines the radars that countries share. Coverage depends on which national radars are included: some areas may be empty even when it rains.

Radar shows the present; it is not a forecast.
topics.how_to_read: Light colours = light rain; yellow/orange/red = heavy rain or thunderstorms. Movement between frames shows where the rain is heading.

topics.title: Layer: sea surface temperature
topics.short: Daily map of the actual sea surface temperature (JPL MUR, about 1 km), in °C.
topics.body: The raw sea surface temperature, not the anomaly. The tropics are always warm, so this map shows where the water is hot, not where it is unusual. Use the anomaly layer to see El Nino.
topics.how_to_read: Colour scale from purple/blue (cold) to red/white (hot). Around Samui, water above about 30 °C for weeks stresses corals.

topics.title: Layer: sea surface temperature anomaly
topics.short: Daily map of how much warmer or cooler the sea is than normal (JPL MUR, about 1 km). The red tongue along the equatorial Pacific is El Nino.
topics.body: This layer is the GHRSST Level 4 MUR sea surface temperature anomaly from NASA JPL, shown through NASA GIBS. It blends many satellites into a daily, gap-free map.
topics.how_to_read:
- Red / orange: warmer than normal. Deep red = several °C above.
- Blue: cooler than normal.
- White / pale: near normal.

Use the legend image for exact values. Look for: the warm tongue along the equator in the eastern Pacific (El Nino); warm patches in the Gulf of Thailand (marine heatwave, coral stress).

topics.title: Layer: soil moisture (SMAP)
topics.short: How much water is in the soil down to about 1 m (the root zone), from NASA's SMAP satellite with a land model. Often 2-3 days behind.
topics.body:
SMAP measures the moisture of the top few centimetres of soil from space; the Level 4 product combines it with a land model to estimate water in the root zone (the layer plants draw from).

Dry soils are one of the first signs of an El Nino drought on land, before reservoirs drop.
topics.how_to_read: Brown/orange = dry, green/blue = wet (see legend). Compare with a few weeks earlier using the date slider.

topics.title: Layer: true-colour image (VIIRS, MODIS)
topics.short: A daily "photo" from space as the eye would see it (Suomi NPP VIIRS or Terra MODIS). Shows clouds, smoke plumes and haze.
topics.body:
These satellites orbit over the poles and image each place about once a day, in strips (swaths). Where strips meet, you can see seams or gaps. MODIS Terra passes in the morning; VIIRS in the early afternoon.

Brown-grey smudges over land or sea are often smoke or haze; bright white is cloud.
topics.how_to_read: White = clouds. Grey/brown veil = smoke or haze. Blue-green swirls in water = sediment or plankton. Black stripes = no data for that day.

topics.title: Level history and engine versions
topics.short: Each history point records the engine version; points from before the 24 Sep 2026 audit are annotated.
topics.body:
`/api/local/history` rows are {evaluated_at, level, level_key, engine_version, note?}. Version 3 (from 24 September 2026) labels every value as observed / forecast / model analysis / reanalysis / bulletin. Rows written by version 2 keep their level (it was computed with the same thresholds) and carry a note saying that engine did not label forecasts.

Limits. The history keeps the last 1000 points (a new point when the level changes, otherwise every 30 minutes).
topics.how_to_read: The level line is continuous across versions; the note only warns that older explanations may have called a forecast date 'observed'.
topics.why_it_matters: Nothing in the history is rewritten after the fact, and nothing misleading is shown without a warning.

topics.title: Limitations and disclaimer
topics.short: This is a personal monitoring tool, not an official warning service. For warnings and evacuation orders, follow the TMD and the DDPM (hotline 1784) and local authorities.
topics.body:
What this dashboard is: a place that gathers public data about El Nino and about Koh Samui, and explains it with transparent rules.

What it is not:

- Not an official warning service. It does not replace the Thai Meteorological Department (TMD, hotline 1182), the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM, hotline 1784), the province, the PWA or the ferry operators.
- Not a forecast of its own. It relays forecasts from others, and they can be wrong.
- Not complete. Some things are not tracked automatically (island reservoir levels, the PWA rotation schedule, ferry timetables). Sources can fail; when they do, the app says so.
- Not medical advice.

The risk thresholds are the app's own choices, based on official scales (TMD rain classes, Thai PCD PM2.5 bands, heat index bands, Beaufort, NOAA Coral Reef Watch) and documented on this page. They are a planning aid.

If official instructions and this app disagree, follow the official instructions.

topics.title: Live webcams -- see it with your own eyes
topics.short: Public live cameras (beaches, piers, streets, buoys, satellites) to check conditions yourself; each shows whether it is live, stale or offline.
topics.body:
A curated list of public cameras: beach, pier and street streams on Koh Samui, the ferry route (Koh Phangan, Koh Tao), wider Thailand, the El Nino "front line" (Peru / Ecuador coast, Australia, Indonesia), NOAA buoy cameras in the open Pacific, and satellite "space cams". Every camera is published by its owner for public viewing (a venue's own YouTube channel, a webcam portal, a government agency).

Limits.

- A camera sees a few hundred metres to a few km. It is a spot check, not a forecast.
- Streams lag 5-60 s; still images lag 10-60 min (satellites) up to hours (buoys).
- At night most cams show little or nothing (beach cams go dark, true-colour satellite images are black, buoy cams stop). Use the infrared satellite image at night.
- Rain on the lens, sun glare and zoom make waves look smaller or bigger than they are.
- Venues move, rename or stop streams without notice; a `reachable` stream can still be an off-air placeholder. Official warnings (TMD, Marine Department) always win.
- No airport, Nathon pier or Donsak pier camera published by its owner was found; Windy webcams (needs a free key) may add some near Samui.
topics.how_to_read:
- Status badge (checked every 30-60 min):
  - `live` -- a still image with a timestamp younger than the cam's limit (buoys 3 h, satellites 1 h). The age is shown next to it.
  - `online` -- the provider's own page says the stream is up (SkylineWebcams).
  - `reachable` -- the stream is still published and embeddable, but we cannot tell from outside whether it is broadcasting right now: the player will show it.
  - `stale` -- the newest image is older than the limit. Treat it as a photo of the past, not of now.
  - `offline` / `error` -- removed, marked offline by the provider, or the check failed. "Last OK" says when it last worked.
- Mode: `proxy` = still image we may show directly (NOAA, JMA); `embed` = the owner's own player (YouTube, Windy); `link` = open the official page (the provider does not allow reuse, e.g. SkylineWebcams).
- Why tells you what the camera is good for (e.g. "sea state toward Koh Phangan").
topics.why_it_matters: Forecasts and warnings tell you what is expected; a camera shows what is happening. Before a ferry, a look at the north-coast and Big Buddha cams shows whether the strait is white with breaking waves. In a flood or heavy-rain event the Chaweng and Lamai street cams show standing water. Haze (from fires in El Nino dry seasons) shows as a milky horizon.

topics.title: Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO)
topics.short: A pulse of tropical clouds and rain that travels east around the equator every 30-60 days.
topics.body:
NOAA PSL's real-time OLR MJO index (ROMI), daily: two components (mjo_romi_pc1, mjo_romi_pc2) and their combined strength mjo_romi_amplitude.

Limits. Published with a delay of about 5 days. The MJO is a short-term signal and does not change the season's overall El Nino tendency.
topics.how_to_read: Amplitude above 1 = an active MJO, below 1 = weak or absent. The two components together say where the active phase is (Indian Ocean, Maritime Continent, western Pacific, ...). We store the numbers; the phase diagram is on the source page.
topics.why_it_matters: When the active MJO passes over the Indian Ocean and Maritime Continent, southern Thailand often gets a wetter 1-3 week spell, even during El Nino; its westerly wind bursts over the Pacific can also strengthen El Nino and help tropical storms form.

topics.title: Map basics (boxes, zones, home circle)
topics.short: The map combines vector data (Nino boxes, typical El Nino impact zones, the 800 km circle around Samui, events, buoys, news) with one optional satellite layer.
topics.body:
What you see on the Map page:

- Nino boxes (red outlines): the Nino regions. Nino 3.4 is highlighted.
- Impact zones (orange = usually drier, blue = usually wetter during El Nino): typical patterns, not this year's forecast (see Teleconnections).
- Home circle (blue dashed): 800 km around Koh Samui. Events inside it are counted as "near".
- Events: GDACS and EONET hazards, FIRMS fires. Clusters show a number; zoom in to split them.
- Buoys (green dots): TAO buoys with a recent reading.
- One satellite layer at a time, with a date slider and an opacity control.

Satellite layers show the latest day the provider actually has. Some products are one or more days behind (soil moisture often 2-3 days).

topics.title: Map event filters
topics.short: Show only some disaster types, sources or alert levels, a date range, a map box, or events within a distance of a point.
topics.body:
Filters on the map events (cyclones, floods, droughts, fires, volcanoes, bleaching, ...): category, source (GDACS, NASA EONET, NASA FIRMS, Coral Reef Watch), severity (green, orange, red, info), "updated since", a map rectangle, and "within N km of a point" (default: the home radius, 800 km, around Koh Samui).

Limits. Positions are a single point per event (a cyclone's latest position, a fire cluster's centre); a large flood or drought covers far more than its dot. Closed events disappear on the next update; anything unseen for 30 days is deleted.
topics.how_to_read:
- Severity colours: GDACS green/orange/red are official alert levels (red = likely need for international help). For NASA FIRMS fires the colour is the number of satellite detections in 24 h (green < 25, orange >= 25, red >= 100), not an alert.
- "Within N km" results show the distance to the point.
- A rectangle that crosses the 180 degree line (Pacific) is handled.
topics.why_it_matters: The question for Koh Samui is "is anything dangerous close to us", which the distance filter answers directly, while the rest of the map shows the El Nino pattern worldwide.

topics.title: Map of the places
topics.short: The compared places on a world map, coloured by their current level. Personal-list places are drawn with a dashed outline.
topics.body: Click a marker for its name, coordinates, elevation and current level. The home place (Maenam) is marked. Distances between places are great-circle distances.

related.title: Adding a place (search, server list, personal list)

topics.title: Marine heatwave
topics.short: A period of days to months when the sea is unusually warm for the season. El Nino years often bring marine heatwaves to Southeast Asian seas.
topics.body:
A marine heatwave is like a heatwave on land, but in the ocean: the sea surface stays much warmer than usual for the season for days to months.

Around Samui, a marine heatwave means coral bleaching risk, stressed fisheries, and warmer, more humid nights on land. Coral Reef Watch's DHW is the best single measure of its effect on reefs.
topics.how_to_read: On the Map, the SST anomaly layer shows it as orange/red around the Gulf of Thailand.

sources.title: NOAA Coral Reef Watch -- Degree Heating Week

topics.title: Measured air quality (Air4Thai)
topics.short: Hourly PM2.5, PM10 and Thai AQI measured at government stations in southern Thailand.
topics.body:
The Pollution Control Department's Air4Thai network. The app keeps the stations within 300 km of Samui; the nearest is Surat Thani (about 87 km). Koh Samui itself has no station. Series air4thai_<station>_pm25 and _pm10 (ug/m3) and _aqi; status key air4thai_samui = nearest station.

Limits. The nearest station is on the mainland; Samui's air is usually cleaner thanks to sea breezes. A station can stop reporting for hours; its timestamp is shown.
topics.how_to_read: Thai AQI bands: 0-25 very good (blue), 26-50 good (green), 51-100 moderate (yellow), 101-200 starting to affect health (orange), above 200 affects health (red). PM2.5 above 37.5 ug/m3 (24-hour) is above Thailand's standard. A missing value means the station does not measure that pollutant.
topics.why_it_matters: El Nino dry seasons bring more fires in Sumatra, Borneo and mainland South-East Asia and so more haze. These are real measurements, a check on the model forecast (CAMS) used for Samui.

topics.title: MEI.v2 (Multivariate ENSO Index)
topics.short: A combined ENSO index from NOAA PSL that blends 5 ocean and atmosphere variables over the tropical Pacific. Positive = El Nino-like.
topics.body:
MEI.v2 looks at the whole coupled system at once, not just ocean temperature. It combines 5 variables over the tropical Pacific (30° S-30° N, 100° E-70° W): sea-level pressure, sea surface temperature, east-west surface wind, north-south surface wind, and outgoing longwave radiation (a satellite measure of cloudiness).

It is computed for 12 overlapping 2-month "seasons" (DJ, JF, FM...) against a 1980-2018 reference period. The result is in standard deviations, like the NOAA SOI but with the opposite sign: positive = El Nino-like.
topics.how_to_read: A high MEI together with a high ONI means ocean and atmosphere agree: the El Nino is well "coupled", which usually means stronger impacts.

sources.title: NOAA PSL -- Multivariate ENSO Index version 2 (MEI.v2)

topics.title: Met Office global and tropical anomalies
topics.short: hadcrut5_global_anom, hadsst4_global_anom, hadsst4_tropics_anom.
topics.body:
Monthly departures from 1961-1990 in the Met Office Hadley Centre records: global land + sea (HadCRUT5), global sea surface and tropical (30S-30N) sea surface (HadSST4).

Limits. Monthly, about 4-8 weeks behind.
topics.how_to_read: degC above 1961-1990; HadCRUT5 rows carry a 95 % range in meta.ci95.
topics.why_it_matters: Independent confirmation of NASA/NOAA; the tropical sea series tracks El Nino warmth.

topics.title: Met Office HadCRUT5 and HadSST4
topics.short: The UK Met Office's long-running global temperature and sea temperature records.
topics.body:
HadCRUT5 (with the University of East Anglia) is the global land + sea surface temperature record; HadSST4 is sea surface temperature only, from ships and buoys. The app keeps the global HadCRUT5, the global HadSST4 and the tropical HadSST4 (30S-30N).

Limits. Monthly, released around the end of the next month. Version numbers in the file names change a few times a decade; the source then shows an error until updated.
topics.how_to_read: degC above 1961-1990. HadCRUT5 carries a 95 % range. July 2026 HadCRUT5: +1.10; August 2026 HadSST4 global +1.14, tropics +1.11.
topics.why_it_matters: An independent check on NASA and NOAA. The tropical sea series shows the El Nino warmth directly.

topics.title: Model vs observation
topics.short: Some values are measured (buoys, rain gauges, satellites); many are computed by models (forecasts, CAMS air quality, ERA5). Models cover everywhere but can be wrong locally.
topics.body:
Three kinds of data in this app:

- Observations: measured by an instrument (TAO buoys, island rain gauges, satellite SST). Real, but only where and when the instrument is.
- Reanalysis (ERA5): past weather rebuilt by combining millions of observations with a weather model. Complete and consistent, but smoothed over about 25 km cells, so it can under-estimate local downpours on a small island.
- Forecasts and model analyses (Open-Meteo weather and marine, CAMS air quality, ECMWF seasonal): computed. Excellent for trends and warnings, less exact for one spot and one hour.

Samui is small compared with most model grid cells, so treat model values as "the area around Samui".

topics.title: Monthly climate charts (1991-2020 normals)
topics.short: Average temperature, rain and sunshine for each month of the year, per place (ERA5, 1991-2020). Lines overlay the places so seasons can be compared.
topics.body: Temperature: mean of daily means, with the average daily max and min available in the table view. Rain: mean monthly total in mm. Sunshine: hours of sunshine per month, computed by Open-Meteo from modelled solar radiation (not a sunshine recorder), so it can read higher than station records: use it to compare places with each other. ERA5 is a ~30 km reanalysis: it is good for comparing places, less precise for local extremes.
topics.why_it_matters: The charts show when each place is at its best and worst: the Samui monsoon (October-December), the Normandy winter drizzle, the Russian deep freeze (December-February).

topics.title: Monthly rain and heat charts (aligned by water year)
topics.short: Every event drawn on the same 12-month axis from June of the developing year to May of the next, with the 1991-2020 monthly normal as a band and 2026 as the thick line that stops at the last complete month.
topics.body:
The horizontal axis is the island's water year: June to September (southwest monsoon, the event grows), October to December (northeast monsoon, the refill), January to May (the dry season after the peak). "Y" is the year the event started, "Y+1" the next one.

- Rain chart: monthly ERA5 rain in mm for each event; the shaded band is the 1991-2020 normal of the same month (the light band spans 75% to 125% of it). A line under the band in Oct-Dec means a weak refill; under it in Feb-Apr, a hard dry season.
- Heat chart: the hottest feels-like day of each month; the dashed line is the 1991-2020 normal of that monthly maximum. The 39 °C reference line is the risk engine's heat "watch" threshold.

Use the legend to hide or show events; hover or tap a month for every event's value. "Show table" gives the same numbers as text.
topics.how_to_read: Look for where a line leaves the band and how long it stays out. The 2026 line only covers complete months (a month needs at least 25 valid days), so it ends before the newest partial month.
topics.why_it_matters: The shape of the year matters more than one total: 2015-16 had a normal refill and still a very dry Feb-Apr; 1991-92 and 2009-10 were dry from October on.
