topics.title: NASA dataset freshness
topics.short: Newest file time and lag of 11 NASA datasets behind our maps.
topics.body:
Status key nasa_dataset_latency {checked_at, datasets: [{id, title, time_end, lag_h, late, why}]}.

Limits. Metadata only.
topics.how_to_read: lag_h = hours between the end of the newest data and the check. late = true when the lag exceeds the normal delay for that product.
topics.why_it_matters: Explains a stale map: NASA itself may be behind.

topics.title: NASA dataset freshness (CMR)
topics.short: How many hours old the newest file of each key NASA dataset is.
topics.body:
NASA's catalogue (CMR) lists every file (granule) of every dataset. Every 3 hours the app asks for the newest one of 11 datasets behind our maps and series: MUR and OISST sea temperature, GPM IMERG rain, SMAP soil moisture, GRACE-FO water storage, Sentinel-6 and NASA-SSH sea level.

Limits. It checks metadata only, not the files themselves. GRACE products are by design months behind.
topics.how_to_read: For each dataset: the time its newest data ends, the lag in hours, and 'late' when the lag is beyond what is normal for that product (e.g. 12 h for 30-minute rain, 72 h for daily sea temperature, months for GRACE).
topics.why_it_matters: When a map layer looks old, this tells you whether it is NASA that is behind (nothing to fix here) or our app.

topics.title: NASA Earth Observatory stories
topics.short: NASA's daily satellite image story, kept only when it is about El Nino impacts.
topics.body:
NASA Earth Observatory publishes one explained satellite image per working day. The app keeps the ones about El Nino, drought, heat, fire and haze, floods, storms, coral bleaching, the oceans or Southeast Asia.

Limits. Only the last ~10 stories are in the feed; many days have no matching story, which is normal.
topics.how_to_read: Each item links to the article; titles stay as published.
topics.why_it_matters: Good plain-language explanations with pictures of what El Nino does around the world.

topics.title: NASA EONET natural events
topics.short: NASA's list of ongoing natural events (storms with their tracks, wildfires, volcanoes, floods, ice) linked to satellite imagery. No impact rating.
topics.body:
EONET (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker) is a curated NASA catalogue of natural events that are happening now, each with its location and links to images and sources. Storms come with their track.

Unlike GDACS, EONET does not rate impact. It answers "what is happening where", not "how bad is it for people".

sources.title: NASA EONET -- Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker

topics.title: NASA GIBS (satellite map tiles)
topics.short: NASA's Global Imagery Browse Services: ready-made satellite map tiles (sea temperature, rain, clouds, smoke...) that the Live map draws, one layer at a time.
topics.body:
GIBS is NASA's free tile service for satellite imagery. It serves hundreds of products (MODIS, VIIRS, GPM IMERG, Himawari, SMAP, GHRSST...) as map tiles, one image per day (or per 10 minutes for geostationary satellites). The Live map asks GIBS directly for the tiles of the chosen layer and date; the server only checks the layer list and the newest date GIBS really has.

It is the same imagery you see in NASA Worldview.
topics.how_to_read:
- Each layer has its own colour scale: read the legend under the layer picker.
- Date: most layers are daily and lag 1-3 days (the satellite must pass, then NASA processes the data). "latest" layers (Himawari infrared) are near real time.
- Grey or empty areas mean no data for that day (clouds for surface products, gaps between satellite passes, night for true colour).
topics.why_it_matters: The map layers show the whole picture around Koh Samui (warm sea, rain bands, fire smoke from Sumatra or Borneo) that no single number captures.

sources.title: NASA Earthdata -- Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS)

topics.title: NASA GISTEMP
topics.short: NASA GISS's monthly global temperature record, land plus ocean, since 1880.
topics.body:
The Goddard Institute for Space Studies combines thousands of weather stations and ship/buoy sea temperatures into a global average and publishes how far each month is from the 1951-1980 average.

Limits. Monthly, published around the 10th of the next month, and recent months can be revised slightly. It is a global average, not a forecast for Samui.
topics.how_to_read: Numbers are degC above the 1951-1980 average. August 2026 was +1.40. The yearly tropical band (24S-24N) is published only once a year is complete.
topics.why_it_matters: El Nino releases ocean heat into the air: the global number usually jumps 0.1-0.2 degC a few months after an El Nino peaks. It tells you how exceptional 2026-2027 is.

topics.title: NASA GMAO forecast plumes
topics.short: Latest monthly NASA GEOS-S2S plume charts for the Nino regions and the IOD.
topics.body:
Status key gmao_s2s_plume {release, posted_at, plumes: [{index, title, url}], how_to_read}.

Limits. Images only, monthly.
topics.how_to_read: Thick red line = average forecast; dashed lines = individual starts. Above +0.5 = El Nino, above +1.5 = strong. For the IOD, above +0.4 = positive IOD (drier SE Asia).
topics.why_it_matters: A NASA opinion on how long and how strong El Nino stays.

topics.title: NASA GMAO GEOS-S2S forecast plumes
topics.short: NASA's own seasonal model forecast of the Nino regions and the Indian Ocean Dipole.
topics.body:
NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office runs the GEOS-S2S-3 coupled model several times a month and publishes plume charts once a month: Nino 3.4, 3, 4, 1+2 and the Indian Ocean Dipole for the next 9 months.

Limits. Images only: NASA does not publish the numbers in a machine-readable form, so none are extracted. Released early each month (September 2026 posted on 2 Sep).
topics.how_to_read: Each dashed line is one model start date, the thick red line their average. Values are degC from normal. The September 2026 release keeps Nino 3.4 near +3.5 to +3.8 through December before a slow decline.
topics.why_it_matters: A third independent forecast next to NOAA/IRI and ECMWF. The Indian Ocean Dipole chart matters too: a positive IOD together with El Nino deepens drought over Southeast Asia.

topics.title: NASA GRACE-FO drought maps
topics.short: Weekly NASA maps of groundwater and soil-moisture drought over Asia.
topics.body:
The GRACE-FO satellites weigh the water stored on land by measuring tiny changes in Earth's gravity. NASA Goddard blends this with a land model and the University of Nebraska's Drought Mitigation Center publishes weekly maps. The app keeps the Asia maps: shallow groundwater, root-zone soil moisture and surface soil moisture.

Limits. The model spreads GRACE's coarse (~300 km) measurement to 0.25 deg, so small islands like Samui are not resolved. Maps are posted weekly (Monday date).
topics.how_to_read: Colours are wetness percentiles compared with 1948-2012: dark red = drier than 98 % of past weeks (2nd percentile), red <= 5, orange <= 10, tan <= 20, yellow <= 30, white 30-70 = normal, light to dark blue = wetter than normal.
topics.why_it_matters: El Nino droughts empty soils and aquifers over months. On 2026-09-21 the map showed much of Thailand and Indochina in the red/dark-red classes. Groundwater drought lasts long after the rains return and matters for Samui's water supply.

topics.title: NASA POWER for Koh Samui
topics.short: NASA's daily satellite-and-model weather for the Samui grid cell, with 2001-2020 normals.
topics.body:
NASA Langley's POWER service combines the MERRA-2 / GEOS-IT weather reanalysis with CERES satellite sunshine data. The app asks it twice a day for the last 60 days of temperature, rain, humidity, wind and sunshine at 9.512 N 100.013 E, and for the 2001-2020 monthly normals of the same place.

Limits. One grid cell is about 50 km across and mixes sea and land, so it smooths out the island's own showers and hottest afternoons. Use trends, not single days.
topics.how_to_read: Values are daily, in local solar time: degC, mm of rain, % humidity, m/s wind, and kWh per m2 per day of sunshine. Temperature and rain arrive about 2-3 days late, sunshine about 5-7 days late. Missing days are simply absent (NASA marks them -999 and the app never stores those).
topics.why_it_matters: It is an independent second source next to Open-Meteo/ERA5: if both say the last weeks were drier and hotter than normal, the signal is solid. In El Nino years Samui often gets a weaker, later rainy season (normally October-December).

topics.title: NASA POWER vs ERA5 cross-check
topics.short: How closely NASA POWER and Open-Meteo ERA5 agree for Samui, day by day.
topics.body:
For the days both have, the mean difference and mean absolute difference of daily maximum and minimum temperature and rain between NASA POWER and ERA5.

Limits. Both are coarse models; neither is a rain gauge on the island.
topics.how_to_read: Small mean differences (under 1 degC) mean the two reanalyses agree. On 2026-09-24: max temperature +0.6 degC on average over 55 days; rain POWER 290 mm vs ERA5 189 mm.
topics.why_it_matters: When two independent sources agree, a drought or heat signal is more trustworthy.

topics.title: NASA Worldview snapshots
topics.short: Ready-made satellite pictures of Samui, the Gulf of Thailand, SE Asia haze and the Pacific El Nino.
topics.body:
NASA Worldview can render any GIBS satellite layer as one image for a chosen area and day. Every 6 hours the app builds 5 such images, downloads each one to make sure it really contains data (an empty day is a tiny black picture), and lists only the good ones.

Limits. Polar-orbiting satellites pass once or twice a day; clouds hide the ground in true colour. If a day has no data the previous day is used, and the date says so.
topics.how_to_read: Each picture carries its date (usually yesterday, the last complete satellite day) and a link to open the same view in Worldview to zoom and change the day.
topics.why_it_matters: A quick look without opening the map: storms around the island, smoke drifting in from Sumatra/Borneo fires, and the band of warm water along the equator that is El Nino.

topics.title: News and posts filters
topics.short: Narrow the feed by type, source, language, tag, date, location or text; chips show how many items each choice has.
topics.body:
Server-side filters on the news / social / official feed: kind (official, news, social, research), source, language, tag (enso, drought, flood, storm, heat, haze, bleaching, thailand, samui, ...), a text search, a date range, and "has a map location". Several values can be picked in each filter.

Limits. Tags come from keyword matching on titles and summaries, so an article can be missed or mis-tagged. Map positions of news are approximate (place named in the text, else the publisher's country). News and social items older than 180 days are removed.
topics.how_to_read:
- Within one filter, items matching ANY chosen value are shown (e.g. tags samui OR flood).
- Different filters combine with AND (e.g. kind = news AND language = th).
- The number on each chip is how many items you would get by adding that value, given your other filters.
- Dates are the publication date, or the date we fetched the item when the source gives none.
topics.why_it_matters: The feed mixes agencies, press and social media in many languages. Filtering to "official" or to the "samui" tag separates what agencies say from noise.

sources.title: GDELT news search (one of the feed sources)

topics.title: News and social signals
topics.short: Articles and posts collected from news search, agency feeds and public social networks. Useful for local, early reports; unreliable as measurements, so they carry little weight.
topics.body:
The News page gathers official bulletins, press articles and public posts about El Nino and about Samui/Thailand. Titles stay in their original language.

Why low weight in the risk level:

- Articles repeat each other; one event can produce dozens of stories.
- Old stories get re-shared.
- Keyword matching cannot tell "no water shortage expected" from "water shortage".
- Posts can be rumours.

What they are good for: local, human reports (a village without water, a road flooded, ferries stopped) that no dataset captures. Always check them against official sources (TMD, PWA, DDPM, ferry operators).

topics.title: Night lights (VIIRS Day/Night Band)
topics.short: Last night's lights seen from space.
topics.body:
Radiance measured by the VIIRS Day/Night Band on NOAA-20 around 1:30 am.

Limits. Clouds block the view; moonlight brightens clouds and sea.
topics.how_to_read: nW/cm2/sr from 0 to about 38: brighter = more light. Compare the same place on several clear nights.
topics.why_it_matters: After a storm, a town that goes dark on a clear night suggests a power cut.

topics.title: Nino 1+2
topics.short: The box off Peru and Ecuador (0-10° S, 90-80° W). It warms first and most in eastern Pacific El Ninos, and swings a lot from week to week.
topics.body:
Nino 1+2 is the smallest and most eastern box, right along the South American coast. It reacts fast, so it is noisy. A warm Nino 1+2 alone (a "coastal El Nino") brings heavy rain to Peru and Ecuador but may have little effect on Asia.

In September 2026 the CPC reported Nino 1+2 at +3.4 °C.

sources.title: NCAR Climate Data Guide -- Nino SST indices

topics.title: Nino 3
topics.short: The eastern equatorial Pacific box (5° N-5° S, 150-90° W). The Japan Meteorological Agency defines El Nino with it.
topics.body:
Nino 3 covers the eastern half of the equatorial Pacific. It was the main El Nino index before Nino 3.4 took over at NOAA. The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) still uses it: see JMA El Nino outlook (Japan).

In September 2026 the CPC reported Nino 3 at +2.5 °C.

sources.title: NCAR Climate Data Guide -- Nino SST indices
JMA -- Monitoring and Prediction of El Nino (definition, PDF)

topics.title: Nino 3.4
topics.short: The average sea temperature anomaly of the box 5° N-5° S, 170° W-120° W. It is the main number used to define El Nino.
topics.body:
The Nino 3.4 index is the sea surface temperature anomaly averaged over the Nino 3.4 box. It sits where changes in ocean temperature move the tropical rain the most, so it tracks ENSO impacts well.

NOAA builds its official indices (ONI, RONI) from it. The app also shows faster versions: weekly (NOAA OISST) and daily (Climate Reanalyzer). See Daily, weekly and monthly values.
topics.how_to_read: +0.5 °C or more = El Nino-like; +1.5 °C or more = strong. One warm week is not an El Nino: the official indices use 3-month averages.
topics.why_it_matters: The app's ENSO factor for Samui uses the highest of the latest ONI and the latest weekly Nino 3.4 anomaly.

sources.title: NCAR Climate Data Guide -- Nino SST indices

topics.title: Nino 4
topics.short: The central and western equatorial Pacific box (5° N-5° S, 160° E-150° W). It warms most in "central Pacific" El Ninos.
topics.body:
Nino 4 sits near the date line, on the edge of the warm pool. Its temperature changes less than the eastern boxes.

In September 2026 the CPC reported Nino 4 at only +0.1 °C: the 2026 event is concentrated in the east.

sources.title: NCAR Climate Data Guide -- Nino SST indices

topics.title: NINO.WEST (western Pacific warm pool)
topics.short: Sea surface temperature anomaly of the western Pacific warm pool east of the Philippines (JMA).
topics.body:
JMA's NINO.WEST index is the monthly SST anomaly over Eq-15N, 130E-150E. The same collector also stores JMA's NINO.3 (5N-5S, 150W-90W), JMA's main El Nino index. Series nino_west_jma_anom, nino3_jma_anom (degC).

Limits. Monthly, preliminary for the latest month.
topics.how_to_read: During El Nino the warm pool usually cools relative to normal while NINO.3 warms. A cool warm pool means less rising air and fewer rain clouds near the Philippines and South-East Asia.
topics.why_it_matters: Less convection over the western Pacific is one of the ways El Nino reduces rainfall over Thailand and shifts where typhoons form.

topics.title: NOAA BuoyCAMs -- cameras on buoys in the open Pacific
topics.short: NOAA cameras on weather buoys in the open Pacific; daylight photos about once an hour.
topics.body:
Cameras mounted on NOAA National Data Buoy Center weather buoys. Each image is a strip of 6 photos taken at the same time in different directions from the buoy, hundreds of km from land (Hawaii, US west coast, Gulf of Alaska, Bering Sea). NOAA publishes them as US public-domain data, so we can show the image itself.

Limits.

- There are no BuoyCAMs on the equatorial TAO array or in the Gulf of Thailand.
- A single photo per hour in daylight; salt on the lens, tilt from waves.
- For numbers (sea temperature, wind, waves) use the buoy data on the Ocean page.
topics.how_to_read:
- The time in the file name is UTC; "age" tells you how old the photo is.
- Whitecaps and foam = strong wind; long smooth swell lines = distant storms.
- Photos are taken about once an hour in daylight only. At night (buoy local time) the newest photo is from the evening before and is marked `stale`.
- `offline` = NOAA currently lists no photo for that buoy (camera fault or maintenance).
topics.why_it_matters: They show the real Pacific the El Nino data comes from. The Hawaii buoys (51000- 51004, 51101) sit in the subtropical Pacific; during El Nino the central Pacific warms and storms shift east, which changes what these cameras see. They are context, not a Koh Samui signal.

topics.title: NOAA Climate at a Glance
topics.short: NOAA's official monthly temperature departures for the globe and for Asia.
topics.body:
NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information publish monthly anomalies from their NOAAGlobalTemp dataset for the globe (land + ocean) and for each continent.

Limits. Monthly, around the 10th of the next month. Continental values are for land only.
topics.how_to_read: degC above the 1901-2000 average (a different, older baseline than NASA's and the Met Office's, so the numbers are higher). August 2026: globe +1.32, Asian land +1.75.
topics.why_it_matters: Shows how the El Nino year ranks against the record for the globe and for Asia.

topics.title: NOAA Coral Reef Watch
topics.short: NOAA's satellite monitoring of heat stress on coral reefs. The app follows the Gulf of Thailand stations (Samui is in the western Gulf station).
topics.body:
Coral Reef Watch uses daily 5 km satellite sea temperatures to estimate how much heat stress reefs are under. For each "virtual station" it gives the SST, the anomaly, the Degree Heating Weeks and a bleaching alert level.

Coral bleaching: when water stays too warm for too long, corals expel the tiny algae living in them and turn white. They can recover if the heat ends soon; long or intense stress kills them.

The product is daily and one day behind.

topics.title: NOAA ENSO Alert System (Watch, Advisory)
topics.short: NOAA's official ENSO status, updated monthly: Watch (El Nino likely within 6 months), Advisory (El Nino is here), Final Advisory (it has ended).
topics.body:
NOAA's Climate Prediction Center (CPC) publishes an ENSO Diagnostic Discussion every month (usually the second Thursday) with a status line:

- El Nino Watch: conditions are favourable for El Nino to develop within the next six months.
- El Nino Advisory: El Nino conditions are observed and expected to continue.
- Final El Nino Advisory: El Nino conditions have ended.
- Not active: none of the above.

The same words exist for La Nina.

"El Nino conditions" means: a one-month relative Nino 3.4 anomaly of +0.5 °C or more, an expectation that the 3-month RONI threshold will be met, AND an atmospheric response typical of El Nino over the equatorial Pacific.
topics.how_to_read: A Watch is a forecast; an Advisory is an observation. The Advisory stays in force until conditions end, then a Final Advisory closes the event.
topics.why_it_matters: As of 10 September 2026 the status is El Nino Advisory, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event in late 2026 and early 2027.

topics.title: NOAA global and Asia monthly anomalies
topics.short: ncei_global_anom and ncei_asia_land_anom.
topics.body:
NOAA NCEI monthly temperature departures for the globe (land + ocean) and Asian land.

Limits. Monthly; continental values are land only.
topics.how_to_read: degC above 1901-2000 (an older baseline, so numbers look higher than NASA's).
topics.why_it_matters: Ranks the El Nino year for the globe and for Asia.

topics.title: NOAA monthly climate reports
topics.short: NOAA's monthly global climate, global drought and tropical cyclone reports.
topics.body:
Every month NOAA NCEI publishes 'State of the Climate' reports. The app keeps the global ones: temperature and rain, drought, and tropical cyclones.

Limits. Monthly; the national (US) reports are skipped.
topics.how_to_read: Each item has the headline numbers and a link to the full report.
topics.why_it_matters: Expert summaries that mention ENSO's role and regional extremes, including Asia.

topics.title: Observed, forecast, model analysis, reanalysis, bulletin
topics.short: Every number says what kind of value it is: measured, predicted, modelled or announced.
topics.body:
Each factor, exit signal, latest value and status document carries a `kind`:
- observed: measured by a station, gauge, buoy or satellite, or an index computed from measurements (ONI, RONI, weekly Nino 3.4, SOI, MEI, Degree Heating Weeks, Air4Thai PM2.5).
- forecast: a model prediction. Today's daily total or maximum is also a forecast, because the day is not over.
- model_analysis: a weather model's own estimate of a past hour or day (Open-Meteo past days, CAMS air quality before now). Not a measurement.
- reanalysis: ERA5, past weather rebuilt from all observations by a model, about 5 days behind. Used against the 1991-2020 normal.
- bulletin: an agency statement (NOAA CPC status, TMD warning, PWA notice, GDACS alert).

Limits. Model analyses and reanalyses are smoothed over 25-50 km grid cells: they miss local showers. Only the ThaiWater gauges and Air4Thai stations are true local measurements, and Koh Samui has no Air4Thai station.
topics.how_to_read: A forecast never has an 'observed' date: its `observed_at` is empty and `valid_for` gives the day it predicts. For example 'forecast max feels-like 37.2 °C on Wed 30 Sep (Open-Meteo, fetched 24 Sep 20:09 ICT)' is a prediction made on 24 September for 30 September.
topics.why_it_matters: A measured flood and a forecast of rain call for different actions. Mixing them up can make you act too late or panic for nothing.

topics.title: Oceanic Kelvin wave
topics.short: A slow, huge underwater wave that travels east along the equator in 2-3 months. A "downwelling" one carries warm water east and can start or boost an El Nino.
topics.body:
When the trade winds weaken or a westerly wind burst blows, the thick warm layer in the western Pacific starts to slide east along the equator. It moves as a wave that you cannot see at the surface (the sea surface rises only a few centimetres) but that pushes the Thermocline down by tens of metres.

- A downwelling Kelvin wave pushes the thermocline down. Cold water cannot come up, so the surface warms. It favours El Nino.
- An upwelling Kelvin wave does the opposite: the thermocline rises and the surface cools.

A Kelvin wave takes about 2 to 3 months to cross the Pacific. That delay is useful: forecasters see it coming.

topics.title: Official travel advisories
topics.short: What the UK FCDO, the US State Department and France Diplomatie currently say about each country, with the date of their last update and a link. Shown as published, not rated.
topics.body:
These are the official, regularly updated government pages. The row quotes their headline (for example "Level 4: Do Not Travel" or "Advises against all travel to the whole country") and the date, and links to the full page. France Diplomatie text stays in French.

They cover security, politics, sanctions, health and entry rules, which the climate data cannot. Other decisive factors (cost of living, visas and residence, healthcare, banking, family) are not in this data: check them separately.
topics.why_it_matters: Advisories affect insurance, flights, banking and consular help. A "do not travel" advice usually voids travel insurance.

topics.title: Official weather warnings per place
topics.short: France: Meteo-France vigilance via Meteoalarm (yellow, orange, red). Russia: the Hydrometcenter daily bulletin of dangerous weather. Thailand: TMD bulletins.
topics.body:
- France (Calvados): Meteo-France publishes its vigilance to Meteoalarm (EUMETNET), read here without a key. An empty feed means no yellow, orange or red warning (green). The Meteo-France API itself needs a key, so it is not used.
- Russia (Vladimir Oblast): the Hydrometcenter of Russia bulletin lists dangerous and adverse weather by federal district. The page shows the sentences that name the region (in Russian, as published). Keyword rule: named = Watch; named with wording such as "very heavy", "hurricane", "severe frost" = Prepare.
- Thailand (Maenam): TMD bulletins for the Gulf side / Surat Thani, collected by the Koh Samui watch.

Always follow the national service when it issues a warning.
topics.why_it_matters: Official warnings are the reference for immediate danger; this page only relays them.

rows: orange / severe wording / TMD heavy rain, waves, storm

topics.title: ONI (Oceanic Nino Index)
topics.short: The 3-month running average of the Nino 3.4 sea temperature anomaly, published monthly by NOAA. +0.5 °C or more = El Nino threshold.
topics.body:
The ONI is NOAA's long-standing El Nino index. Each value is the average anomaly over three consecutive months, labelled by their initials: JJA = June-July-August (see Season codes (DJF, JJA, SON...)).

- It uses the ERSST ocean dataset (version 6 since 2026) and centred 30-year base periods updated every 5 years.
- Historically, an El Nino "episode" is counted when the ONI is at or above +0.5 °C for at least 5 consecutive overlapping seasons.
- Recent values can be revised for up to two months after they are first posted.

Since 1 February 2026, NOAA uses the relative version, RONI, for official monitoring. The ONI is still published and still shown here, because it is the index most people and older articles refer to.
topics.how_to_read: One point per month on the chart, dated at the centre month (JJA 2026 is plotted at mid-July 2026). The band from -0.5 to +0.5 is neutral.
topics.why_it_matters: The app's ENSO factor for Samui is based on the ONI (plus the weekly Nino 3.4 value): >= +0.5 gives Watch, >= +1.5 gives Prepare.
topics.example: CPC values for 2026: AMJ +0.95, MJJ +1.39, JJA +1.80 °C.

topics.title: Open-Meteo forecasts
topics.short: A free service that serves forecasts from national weather models (ECMWF, DWD ICON, NOAA GFS...), choosing the best model for each place. Used for Samui's weather, waves, air and seasonal outlook.

topics.title: Pacific sea level tilt (east minus west)
topics.short: sla_pacific_east_minus_west = sla_nino34 minus sla_west_pacific.
topics.body:
The difference between the sea level in the central-east equatorial Pacific and in the western Pacific warm pool, in cm.

Limits. A simple two-box difference, not an official index.
topics.how_to_read: Positive and large = the Pacific is tilted the El Nino way (water piled up in the east). On 2026-09-22 it was about +45 cm. Near zero or negative = neutral or La Nina.
topics.why_it_matters: Global sea level rise is in both boxes and cancels out, so this is a clean ENSO signal that reacts to wind changes within days.

topics.title: Past strong El Nino events
topics.short: The three strongest El Ninos since 1950 by ONI peaked at about +2.1 °C (1982-83), +2.4 °C (1997-98) and +2.6 °C (2015-16). 2023-24 peaked at about +2.0 °C.
topics.body:
The Overview page compares the current event with these past events. Values below are the peak 3-month ONI and RONI from the NOAA CPC data files (downloaded 2026-09-24). ONI and RONI differ because RONI removes the warming of the whole tropics (see RONI (Relative Oceanic Nino Index)).

Notes:

- 1982-83: one of the strongest on record; it was not predicted in advance.
- 1997-98: one of the strongest; TMD notes it developed fast and brought drought to Thailand and fires in Indonesia and Malaysia (haze).
- 2015-16: the highest ONI peak in the record; severe drought in Thailand and haze across the region.
- 2023-24: strong by ONI (about +2.0) but only moderate by RONI (+1.4), because the whole tropical ocean was unusually warm at the time. This is exactly why NOAA moved to RONI.

thresholds.note: Source: cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/data/indices/oni.ascii.txt and RONI.ascii.txt. Recent values can be revised for up to two months.

topics.title: Place level (current, 0-4)
topics.short: One level per place for NOW and the next 7 days, from 9 factors (heat, cold, water, flood, storm, air, wildfire, earthquakes, official warnings). Same names as the Samui watch: Normal, Watch, Prepare, Act, Leave.
topics.body:
Each factor is scored 0-4 from real data and shows its value, threshold, source and date. The overall level is:

- R1: the highest factor, each capped (earthquakes at 2 Prepare; cold, water, flood, air, wildfire and warnings at 3; heat and storm can reach 4).
- R3: two physical hazards at 2 Prepare or more at the same time give at least 3 Act.
- If heat, water, flood or storm has no current data, the level is Unknown, never Normal.

For Maenam the detailed Koh Samui watch (with water supply, sea state, ferries...) remains the reference; its level is shown on the Maenam card.
topics.why_it_matters: The current level tells you how each place is doing today. It is not a verdict on the place: a Russian winter cold snap or a Thai dry spell are normal parts of those climates. Use the matrix for the long view.

rows: Water, tropical profile (Maenam): ERA5 rain, 90 days, % of normal
Water, temperate profile (Normandy, Vladimir): 365 d / 180 d / 90 d, % of normal
< 65% / < 50% / never on 90 d alone; >= 100 mm short
> 35 mm in 24 h, or river above its 99th percentile
> 90 mm/24 h or 150 mm/72 h, or a 2-year river flood
>= 150 mm/24 h or 250 mm/72 h, or a 10-year river flood
>= 75 km/h, or a cyclone within 800 km
>= 118 km/h, or orange/red cyclone within 500 km (300 km: Leave)
thresholds.note: Critical factors: heat, water, flood, storm. A factor whose data is too old cannot say Normal: it becomes unknown.

topics.title: Places: sea state near the coast
topics.short: Wave height and sea surface temperature at the sea cell nearest to each place (Open-Meteo marine model). Inland places have none.
topics.body:
For each place on the Places page the app asks the Open-Meteo marine model for the nearest sea grid cell and keeps its wave height (m) and sea surface temperature (°C), recent days and forecast. Places far from the sea (Gorokhovets, for example) get no sea cell and are shown as "inland".

The distance to the chosen cell is a rough indication: the model grid is coarse (about 5-25 km), so a sheltered bay can be calmer than its cell.
topics.how_to_read: Waves below 1.25 m are moderate; 2 m and more stop small boats and fast ferries in the Gulf of Thailand; 3 m and more usually stop the car ferries. Values after today are forecasts.
topics.why_it_matters: For an island (Maenam) the sea decides whether ferries and supplies run; on the mainland it matters for coastal flooding and fishing only.

topics.title: PM2.5 and the Thai bands
topics.short: Tiny particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres (about 1/30 of a hair) that go deep into the lungs. Thailand's 24-hour standard is 37.5 µg/m³ since June 2023.
topics.body:
PM2.5 comes from smoke (forest fires, crop burning), traffic and industry. Because the particles are so small, they reach deep into the lungs and the blood. It is measured in micrograms per cubic metre of air (µg/m³), usually as a 24-hour average.

Thailand tightened its standard on 1 June 2023: the 24-hour limit went from 50 to 37.5 µg/m³, and the red band now starts at 75.1 µg/m³.

thresholds.note: Bands as used by the risk engine (Thai PCD, revised 2023).

topics.title: Preparedness: communication
topics.short: Cell towers go down when the power is out for long. Write key numbers on paper and agree a plan with someone off the island.
topics.body: Keep emergency numbers written down (police 191, ambulance 1669, fire 199, tourist police 1155, DDPM 1784, TMD 1182), a charged phone and power bank, offline maps, and a contact off the island who knows your plan.

sources.title: Thai DDPM -- Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (hotline 1784)

topics.title: Preparedness: departure plan
topics.short: The island can only be left by ferry, boat or plane. When seas exceed about 2 m, crossings are cut. Decide in advance what would make you leave, and keep a go-bag ready.
topics.body: Decide your trigger in advance (for example: water cut for more than 3 days, or level Act with the sea about to close). Keep a go-bag with documents, medicine, cash, a day of water and food, a headlamp and rain gear. See the Exit plan (leaving the island) for routes and departure windows.

sources.title: Thai DDPM -- Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (hotline 1784)

topics.title: Preparedness: documents
topics.short: A rushed departure or a flood leaves no time to look for papers. Keep passport, visa papers and insurance in a waterproof bag, with copies online.
topics.body: Passport, visa or extension papers, insurance policy with its emergency hotline, and prescriptions: originals in a dry bag in one place, copies stored online.

sources.title: American Red Cross -- Survival kit supplies

topics.title: Preparedness: flood and storm
topics.short: The northeast monsoon (October-December) brings Samui's heaviest rain, El Nino or not. Keep documents and electronics high and dry; never cross moving water.
topics.body: Heavy rain on saturated ground floods low roads and can trigger landslides on slopes. Before a storm: tie down or bring in anything that can fly, prepare tarps and rope, charge everything, and follow the TMD and the DDPM (1784). During: avoid flooded roads and slopes; never walk or drive through moving water.

sources.title: Thai DDPM -- Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (hotline 1784)

topics.title: Preparedness: food
topics.short: If ferries stop or the power goes out, island supermarkets empty quickly. Keep food that needs no cooking and little water.
topics.body: A stock of non-perishable food that can be eaten without cooking (canned food, crackers, nuts, dried fruit, ready meals) covers ferry stoppages and power cuts. Choose food that does not need much water to prepare, and rotate it so it does not expire.

sources.title: American Red Cross -- Survival kit supplies

topics.title: Preparedness: haze
topics.short: In El Nino years, fire haze from Indonesia and Malaysia can reach southern Thailand. N95/KN95 masks and one room with a HEPA purifier protect the most.
topics.body: Keep N95 or KN95 masks (not surgical masks) and, if possible, a HEPA air purifier for one room with the windows closed. Check PM2.5 and ASMC alerts when the sky looks hazy.

sources.title: ASMC -- Alert levels for transboundary haze
Air4Thai -- Thai Pollution Control Department air quality

topics.title: Preparedness: health (dengue, medicine)
topics.short: Heat, doubtful water and dengue (more mosquitoes with heat and rain) are the main health risks. Keep 30 days of prescription medicine.
topics.body:
- Dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes, which breed in standing water (including stored water, so cover tanks and containers). Use repellent and nets. The WHO advises paracetamol for pain and fever, and avoiding ibuprofen and aspirin (bleeding risk).
- Water: stored or trucked water can be contaminated; treat it if unsure.
- Medication: keep at least 30 days of prescriptions, with the prescriptions themselves.
- Heat: see Preparedness: heat.

sources.title: WHO fact sheet -- Dengue and severe dengue

topics.title: Preparedness: heat
topics.short: El Nino likely makes March-May 2027 hotter. Above 41 °C feels-like, heat stroke is possible. Plan cool rest, water, oral rehydration salts, and a fan that works without mains power.
topics.body: Avoid exertion between 11:00 and 16:00, drink regularly, use oral rehydration salts (ORS), and check on older people, children and anyone ill. Signs of heat stroke (confusion, hot and red skin that may be dry or damp, fainting) are an emergency: call 1669.

sources.title: US National Weather Service -- Heat index

topics.title: Preparedness: home and pets
topics.short: Preparing the house limits damage; pets are not always accepted on ferries or planes, so check the rules before you need them.
topics.body: Know how to shut off the water valve, the main breaker and the gas bottle. Keep valuables high in flood-prone houses. For pets: carrier, vaccination record and food, and check ferry and airline rules for animals in advance.

topics.title: Preparedness: money
topics.short: Without power or network, cards and ATMs stop working, and ATMs empty fast when everyone leaves. Keep some cash in baht.
topics.body: Keep cash in baht for several days of essentials and for a ticket, plus two cards from different banks.

topics.title: Preparedness: power cuts
topics.short: Monsoon storms and heat waves cause outages. Without power: no fan or air conditioning, no pump for the house tank, no phone charging.
topics.body: Keep power banks charged, headlamps and spare batteries, and a battery-powered fan for hot nights. If you have a generator or solar panel, test it. Remember that many houses need electricity to pump water from the tank.

topics.title: Preparedness: water
topics.short: Water is the first El Nino risk on Samui. WHO: 2.5-3 L per person per day just to survive (drinking and food), 7.5-15 L for basic needs. In the heat, drinking needs rise.
topics.body:
Why: Samui's reservoirs are small, the mainland pipeline covers under half of demand (see Samui's water supply), and a strong El Nino raises the odds of a long, hot dry season.

Reference amounts (WHO Technical Note 9): survival needs of 2.5-3 L per person per day (drinking and food); basic hygiene 2-6 L; basic cooking 3-6 L; total basic needs 7.5-15 L. FEMA advises at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day, and notes that needs can double in hot climates.

Keep a sealed drinking stock, keep the house tank full and clean, and know how to treat water (boiling for 1 minute, or unscented household bleach at the dose on Ready.gov).

sources.title: WHO Technical Note 9 -- How much water is needed in emergencies

topics.title: PTWC tsunami messages
topics.short: The latest message of NOAA's Pacific Tsunami Warning Center.
topics.body:
PTWC (Honolulu) issues information statements, advisories, watches and warnings after significant earthquakes in the Pacific and the South China Sea.

Limits. Only the latest message is kept in the feed; the Pacific feed does not cover the Indian Ocean.
topics.how_to_read: Most messages are 'Information' and say there is no tsunami threat. The category is shown as a tag (information, advisory, watch, warning).
topics.why_it_matters: Context only: the Gulf of Thailand is sheltered, and the Indian Ocean side is covered by the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System and Thailand's NDWC.

topics.title: Public site (read-only)
topics.short: On the public address anyone can read everything, but actions that change the server (running sources, re-evaluating, editing the shared places) are reserved for the owner.
topics.body:
The public site shows the same live data as the owners' own copy. To keep it safe and fair to the data providers, visitors cannot:

- run or verify sources on demand (that would hammer the providers),
- force a re-evaluation of the Koh Samui level,
- add or remove places on the shared Places list,
- save the Preparedness checklist on the server.

Your Preparedness ticks and your personal Places list are kept in this browser instead (they stay after a reload, but not on another device). The owner can sign in with an admin token to get the buttons back.
topics.how_to_read: A note "reserved for the site owner" replaces each hidden button. Everything else works normally.

Adding a place (search, server list, personal list)

topics.title: PWA Samui water notices
topics.short: Official water-supply interruption notices of the PWA Ko Samui branch.
topics.body:
The Provincial Waterworks Authority publishes interruption notices per branch (pipe bursts, planned interruptions asking you to store water, 'water cannot be supplied'). The app reads the Ko Samui branch every 3 hours.

Limits. The rotation schedule and the island reservoirs' levels are not published in a machine-readable form, so they are not tracked. Local announcements on social media are not read.
topics.how_to_read: A notice in force raises the water factor to 'Watch'; a 'water cannot be supplied' notice or one lasting more than 48 hours raises it to 'Prepare'. An empty list means no notice is published, not that supply is guaranteed. Notice texts stay in Thai.
topics.why_it_matters: Samui's supply is tight (about 16,000 m3/day available for 34,000 m3/day of demand in July 2026) and the PWA announced rotating supply from 3 August 2026.

topics.title: Rain as % of normal
topics.short: Rain over the last 30, 60, 90 or 180 days divided by the 1991-2020 average for the same calendar days. 60% means 40% less rain than usual.
topics.body:
The app adds up the rain observed on Samui (ERA5 reanalysis, about 5 days behind) over several windows, and compares each with the 1991-2020 ERA5 normal for exactly the same days of the year.

- 100% = a normal amount.
- Below 75% = drier than normal (the water factor starts at Watch).
- Above 100% = wetter than normal.

Short windows (30 days) react fast but a single storm can swing them. Long windows (180 days) show the slow deficit that empties reservoirs.
topics.how_to_read: Look at both the % and the millimetres: 40% of a dry-season normal of 60 mm is only 36 mm missing, while 60% of a November normal can be over 100 mm missing.

topics.title: Rain right now (IMERG 30-minute)
topics.short: Satellite rain for the latest half hour, over land and sea.
topics.body:
NASA's GPM IMERG Early estimate, 30-minute average, about 4-6 hours behind.

Limits. Satellite estimate: can miss short island showers or overestimate some storms.
topics.how_to_read: mm per hour, scale 0.1 to 53: pale = light rain (<1 mm/h), strongest colours = downpours (>10-20 mm/h).
topics.why_it_matters: Shows storm bands approaching Samui from the sea where no radar reaches.

topics.title: RainViewer (rain radar mosaic)
topics.short: A worldwide mosaic of national weather radars, updated every 10 minutes. The map shows the newest frame and its time.
topics.body: RainViewer collects the images of public weather radars (the Thai Meteorological Department's among them) and joins them into one map. The app asks RainViewer which frames exist and shows the newest past frame; its time is printed with the layer.
topics.how_to_read:
- Colours = rain intensity (light blue light rain, yellow/red heavy rain, purple very heavy or hail).
- Only where a radar reaches (about 200-250 km from each radar). Outside, the map is empty, which does not mean dry.
- Frames are past radar images, not a forecast.
topics.why_it_matters: Radar shows a rain band approaching the Gulf of Thailand in the next hour or two, useful before a ferry crossing or a drive in a monsoon surge.

topics.title: Ranking and weights (decision aid)
topics.short: Score = weighted average of (4 - exposure) over the dimensions that have data, shown as 0-100. You set the weights; by default all are equal. A decision aid only.
topics.body:
How it is computed, with nothing hidden:

- For each place and dimension, suitability = 4 - exposure score (so 4 = best, 0 = worst).
- Score = sum(weight x suitability) / sum(weight x 4) x 100.
- Dimensions without data for a place are left out for that place and listed; compare coverage before trusting a close ranking.
- Weights go from 0 (ignore) to 5 (very important). They are saved in this browser only.

It leaves out everything that is not in this data: cost of living, visas, healthcare, language, family, politics. The official advisories are shown next to it for that reason.
topics.why_it_matters: Different people weigh the same facts differently. The sliders make that explicit instead of hiding it in a single number.
topics.example: If cold matters three times more than heat to you, set Cold to 3 and Heat stress to 1: the ranking changes instantly.

topics.title: Reading a forecast probability
topics.short: A 70% chance of El Nino means that in 10 similar situations, about 7 would end up in El Nino. It is about likelihood, not intensity.
topics.body:
Seasonal forecasts are given as probabilities because the climate has a lot of chaos in it.

- 70% El Nino does not mean "a 70% strong El Nino". It means El Nino is likely, but a 30% chance of something else remains.
- 33% for each of three categories would mean "we have no idea" (all equal).
- Probabilities for impacts (for example "below-normal rain in Thailand") are always less certain than probabilities for El Nino itself, because many other things affect local weather.

topics.title: Regional earthquakes (USGS)
topics.short: Magnitude 4.5+ earthquakes of the last 7 days within 3000 km of Koh Samui.
topics.body:
The USGS global feed of M4.5+ earthquakes, filtered to Sumatra, the Andaman Sea, Myanmar, the Philippines and Indonesia.

Limits. Magnitudes are revised in the first hours. For tsunami warnings in Thailand follow the NDWC / TMD, not this list.
topics.how_to_read: Severity: red = magnitude 7 or more, or the USGS tsunami flag; orange = magnitude 6 or more; green = smaller. The flag means the event is in an area where tsunamis are possible, not that one happened.
topics.why_it_matters: Not an El Nino effect. It is here so that a large regional quake is never missed: the 2004 Sumatra tsunami hit Thailand's Andaman coast (Phuket, Krabi, Khao Lak). Koh Samui is in the Gulf of Thailand, well sheltered from Indian Ocean tsunamis.

topics.title: ReliefWeb humanitarian reports
topics.short: UN and NGO situation reports that mention El Nino or concern Thailand.
topics.body:
ReliefWeb (UN OCHA) collects reports, appeals and assessments from humanitarian organisations. The app reads those of the last 60 days that mention El Nino or are about Thailand.

Limits. Needs a free approved 'appname' from ReliefWeb (set RELIEFWEB_APPNAME); without it the source shows 'needs configuration'.
topics.how_to_read: Each item is an official report with its publishing organisations. Tags mark El Nino and Thailand items.
topics.why_it_matters: Shows how El Nino is affecting food, water and health in the region, and whether Thailand has an active disaster response.

topics.title: River discharge (GloFAS)
topics.short: Daily river flow in m3/s from the Copernicus GloFAS model for the largest river cell near the place, compared with its 2001-2020 flood levels.
topics.body:
GloFAS is a global hydrological model on a 5 km grid. For each place we search 7 x 7 cells (about 15 km) and keep the one with the largest flow, then compute from 2001-2020:

- the 99th percentile of daily flow,
- the 2-year flood (median of the yearly maxima),
- the 10-year flood (90th percentile of the yearly maxima).

The forecast (30 days, ensemble) is compared with these levels. Model flows can differ from gauges, especially for small or regulated rivers and estuaries.
topics.why_it_matters: Spring snowmelt floods (Russia) and long rainy spells (Normandy) show up here days to weeks ahead.

topics.title: RONI (Relative Oceanic Nino Index)
topics.short: NOAA's official ENSO index since 1 February 2026: the Nino 3.4 anomaly minus the average anomaly of the whole tropical ocean (20° S-20° N), as a 3-month mean.
topics.body:
Why it exists: the whole tropical ocean has been warming. With the classic ONI, part of that general warming shows up as "El Nino-like" warmth, and the 30-year baseline struggles to keep up in real time.

What matters for the weather is whether the Nino 3.4 region is warmer than the rest of the tropics, because that contrast is what moves the rain and the winds. RONI measures exactly that:

- Take the Nino 3.4 SST anomaly.
- Subtract the average SST anomaly of the global tropics (20° S to 20° N).
- Rescale so that its variability matches the ONI.
- Average over 3 months.

The thresholds are unchanged: +0.5 °C for El Nino, -0.5 °C for La Nina, 5 consecutive overlapping seasons for a historical episode. NOAA made RONI official through NWS Public Information Statement 26-05, effective 1 February 2026.
topics.how_to_read: Read it like the ONI. RONI is usually a bit lower than ONI when the whole tropics are unusually warm (2023-24: ONI peak +2.0, RONI peak +1.4).
topics.why_it_matters: NOAA now states El Nino strength and forecasts in RONI (for example, the 75% chance of a RONI of +2.5 °C or more in October-December 2026). Note: the app's ENSO factor still uses ONI and the weekly Nino 3.4 value, which run higher than RONI this year (JJA 2026: ONI +1.80, RONI +1.36).

NWS Public Information Statement 26-05 (RONI official from 1 Feb 2026)

topics.title: Running mean (moving average)
topics.short: An average over a window that slides forward in time. It removes short-lived ups and downs so the trend is easier to see.
topics.body:
A 3-month running mean averages months 1-2-3, then 2-3-4, then 3-4-5, and so on. It smooths out week-to-week noise (a passing storm can cool the ocean for a few days).

The price: it lags. A 3-month mean centred on July is only complete at the end of August and is published in early September. That is why the app also shows weekly and daily Nino 3.4 values, which are faster but noisier.

topics.title: Samui daily weather from NASA POWER
topics.short: samui_power_t2m, _t2m_max, _t2m_min, _t2m_anom, _precip, _rh, _wind10m, _solar.
topics.body:
Daily values for the Samui grid cell from NASA POWER: mean, maximum and minimum air temperature at 2 m, rain, relative humidity, wind at 10 m and sunshine energy. samui_power_t2m_anom is the daily mean minus the 2001-2020 mean of that month.

Limits. Grid-cell values (about 50 km), smoother than a real station.
topics.how_to_read: degC, mm, %, m/s, kWh/m2/day. A run of positive anomalies = warmer than usual; rain is best read as 30-day totals (status samui_power).
topics.why_it_matters: Independent check on the Open-Meteo numbers used by the risk engine.

topics.title: Samui last 30 days vs normal (NASA POWER)
topics.short: Rain total and mean temperature of the last 30 days compared with 2001-2020.
topics.body:
Built from NASA POWER: 30-day rain total, the normal total for the same days, the percentage of normal, and the mean temperature with its normal and anomaly.

Limits. Grid-cell values; the normals are 2001-2020, not 1991-2020.
topics.how_to_read: precip_pct_of_normal below ~60 % for several weeks in October-December would be an El Nino-type dry monsoon. At 2026-09-21: 186 mm (111 % of normal), 28.7 degC (+0.7).
topics.why_it_matters: The island's water supply depends on the October-December rains.

topics.title: Samui metrics table and its colours
topics.short: Rain is coloured by % of the 1991-2020 normal (orange under 75%, red under 60%, blue above 125%), heat by feels-like degrees and heat days, dry spells by length. The last row is the median of ENSO-neutral years, the yardstick.
topics.body:
Each event's water year is reduced to six numbers for Koh Samui, all from the ERA5 grid cell that holds Maenam (ERA5 reanalysis):

- Oct-Dec rain: the northeast-monsoon refill, as % of the 1991-2020 normal of the same cell.
- Jan-May rain: the dry season after the El Nino peak.
- Feb-Apr rain: the danger window when the tanks are lowest.
- Max feels-like: the hottest daily maximum feels-like temperature in Jan-May, with its date.
- Days >= 39 °C: days in Jan-May with a feels-like maximum at or above 39 °C (the risk engine's heat "watch" threshold, see Factor: extreme heat).
- Longest dry spell: the longest run of days with less than 1 mm of rain in Jan-May, counted across month ends.

The neutral median row is the median of the same numbers over the water years whose ONI stayed between -0.5 and +0.5 °C from autumn to spring (no El Nino and no La Nina): what a "normal" year looks like in the same data. The count of years (n) is shown.
topics.how_to_read: Read down a column to compare events, and against the neutral row to see what is unusual. A cell shown as "--" with a "loading" note means a month of the ERA5 history is not stored yet; the number is not estimated.
topics.why_it_matters: The Feb-Apr column is the one to watch: in 6 of the 7 events it was under 60% of normal, and that is the window when Samui ran short of water in 2016 and 2024.

rows: serious deficit: the live water factor calls this "prepare"
deficit: the live water factor calls this "watch"
thresholds.note: Heat cells go orange from 39 °C feels-like and red from 40 °C; heat days orange from 3, red from 7; dry spells orange from 30 days, red from 45. Thresholds match the live factors and the takeaways.

topics.title: Samui's water supply
topics.short: Samui relies on small reservoirs, desalination and an undersea pipeline from the mainland. In 2026 a long dry spell led the PWA to rotate supply by zone from 3 August.
topics.body:
What is known (sources linked below):

- Tap water on Samui is run by the PWA (Provincial Waterworks Authority), Ko Samui branch.
- Supply comes from the island's small reservoirs, desalination plants and a pipeline from the Surat Thani mainland.
- According to the PWA as reported in July 2026, the mainland pipeline supplies about 16,000 m³ per day, against an average island demand of about 34,000 m³ per day.
- In late July 2026 a prolonged dry spell, worsened by El Nino, cut clean-water production to about 40% of normal, and the PWA announced supply rotating by zone from 3 August 2026 (Bangkok Post, 29 July 2026). Hotels and businesses bought trucked water.

What the app tracks: PWA Samui interruption notices (from the PWA notice service) and rain vs normal. What it does not track (no machine-readable source): reservoir levels and the rotation schedule. Check PWA Samui announcements directly.
topics.why_it_matters: A system already short in August 2026 enters the 2027 dry season with a very strong El Nino peaking. If the October-December monsoon is weak, shortages in February-April 2027 are likely. This is the single biggest risk for residents who stay.

sources.title: Bangkok Post, 29/07/2026 -- Koh Samui faces water rationing

topics.title: Satellite sea level anomaly (NOAA CoastWatch)
topics.short: Daily sea surface height from radar satellites, averaged over key Pacific boxes, the Gulf of Thailand and the sea around Samui.
topics.body:
Radar altimeters (Sentinel-6, Jason-3, SWOT, Sentinel-3, CryoSat-2) measure the height of the sea surface to a few centimetres. NOAA CoastWatch merges them into a daily 0.25 deg map. Twice a day the app averages the last 15 days over 6 boxes.

Limits. Coastal boxes (Samui, Gulf) are less accurate because altimeters struggle near land. The server is sometimes slow or down; the source then shows an error, never old numbers as new.
topics.how_to_read: Values are cm above the DTU15 mean sea surface (a 1993-2012 reference), so they include roughly 8-10 cm of long-term sea level rise. On 2026-09-22 the Nino 3.4 box was +37 cm and the western Pacific -8 cm.
topics.why_it_matters: El Nino is a sloshing of the Pacific: warm water piles up in the east (sea level up) and drains from the west (sea level down) weeks before surface temperatures peak. Around Samui, higher sea level adds to storm-surge and high-tide flooding risk.

topics.title: Satellite snapshots
topics.short: Verified satellite pictures: Samui, Gulf of Thailand, SE Asia haze, Pacific SST.
topics.body:
Status key snapshots {items: [{id, title, date, url, worldview_url, description}], failed}. Each image was downloaded once and checked to contain data.

Limits. Satellite pictures are from yesterday; clouds hide the ground.
topics.how_to_read: True colour: white = cloud, grey-brown veils = smoke/haze. Aerosol map: yellow to red = thick haze. SST anomaly: red = warmer than normal, blue = cooler; the dark red equatorial band is El Nino.
topics.why_it_matters: A fast visual check of storms, haze and the state of El Nino.

topics.title: Sea level anomaly boxes
topics.short: sla_nino34, sla_nino12, sla_west_pacific, sla_south_china_sea, sla_gulf_thailand, sla_samui_coast.
topics.body:
Daily average satellite sea level in each box: Nino 3.4 (5S-5N, 170W-120W), Nino 1+2 off Peru, the western Pacific warm pool (5S-5N, 130E-160E), the South China Sea, the Gulf of Thailand and the sea just around Koh Samui.

Limits. Near-coast boxes (Samui, Gulf) are noisier: altimeters are less accurate near land.
topics.how_to_read: cm above a 1993-2012 mean surface (includes ~8-10 cm of long-term rise). During a strong El Nino the eastern boxes run +20 to +40 cm and the western Pacific near or below zero.
topics.why_it_matters: Sea level rises in the east Pacific before the surface warming peaks, and a high Gulf of Thailand adds to coastal flooding at high tide and in storms.

topics.title: Sea surface salinity (SMAP)
topics.short: Saltiness of the sea surface, 8-day average.
topics.body:
NASA SMAP radiometer, JPL CAP algorithm, 8-day running mean.

Limits. Less reliable within ~40 km of coasts (so around Samui itself).
topics.how_to_read: PSU, scale 30-40; open ocean ~34-35. Fresher = heavy rain or river water.
topics.why_it_matters: During El Nino the fresh water under the Pacific rain band moves east; in the Gulf of Thailand fresher water follows big rain and river floods.

topics.title: Sea surface temperature (SST)
topics.short: The temperature of the top layer of the ocean, measured by satellites, ships and buoys, in °C.
topics.body:
SST is the temperature of the ocean surface (roughly the top metre). It is measured by satellites (infrared and microwave sensors), ships, drifting buoys and moored buoys such as the TAO array. Products such as NOAA OISST and ERSST blend these into maps.

ENSO is measured mainly with SST in the equatorial Pacific. SST also matters locally: warm water around Samui feeds heavier showers and stresses corals.

topics.title: Season codes (DJF, JJA, SON...)
topics.short: Three letters = three consecutive months, by their initials. DJF = December-January-February; JJA = June-July-August.
topics.body:
ENSO indices and forecasts use overlapping 3-month seasons, named by the first letter of each month:

DJF, JFM, FMA, MAM, AMJ, MJJ, JJA, JAS, ASO, SON, OND, NDJ.

"Overlapping" means each season shares two months with the next one. So a value for JJA and a value for JAS are not independent: they share July and August.

Watch out: DJF starts in December of one year and ends in February of the next. "DJF 2027" in forecasts means December 2026 to February 2027.

topics.title: Season-aware risk rules
topics.short: Some thresholds weigh differently depending on Samui's season.
topics.body:
Samui's rain year: northeast monsoon October-January (November wettest, about half of the year's rain October-December); dry season February-May (February driest); southwest monsoon June-September, when the island is sheltered.

Limits. Normals come from ERA5 (about 30 km cells), which underestimates rain at Samui's stations; comparisons are ERA5 against ERA5, so the bias largely cancels. The 7-day antecedent rain uses model analyses, not gauges.
topics.how_to_read: Water: in the dry season the 180-day rain window (which holds the last monsoon refill) is used if it is worse than the 90-day one; in October-December a rain deficit during a strong El Nino is at least 'Prepare', because the reservoirs refill only then; a rain-only 'Act' needs at least 100 mm really missing, not just a low percentage of a tiny dry-season normal. Flood: heavy rain forecast on ground soaked by 150 mm or more over the past 7 days raises the flood level by one; 250 mm in a week alone is 'Watch'. Sea: TMD wave warnings for the Andaman Sea only are ignored (they do not concern the Gulf).
topics.why_it_matters: El Nino makes the February-April 2027 dry season the water danger window, while floods still come with the northeast monsoon (for example the November-December 2024 floods in the South and the 2011 and 2017 floods).

topics.title: Seasonal outlook for Samui (ECMWF SEAS5)
topics.short: A 6-month forecast of monthly rain and temperature for Samui from the European centre's seasonal model, as a % of the model's own normal.
topics.body:
The Samui page shows the ECMWF SEAS5 seasonal forecast (through Open-Meteo) for the next months. Each month shows expected rain as a percentage of the model's own normal for that month.

Seasonal models do not predict individual storms or rainy days. They predict whether a whole month is likely to be wetter or drier than usual. Coarse grid cells (tens of km) cannot resolve a small island, so treat it as a regional tendency.
topics.how_to_read: Below 100% = drier than normal; below 80% for the next 3 months raises the water factor to at least Watch.

related.title: Forecast uncertainty and the spring barrier

topics.title: Seasonal outlook per place (ECMWF SEAS5)
topics.short: Forecast monthly temperature and rain anomalies for the next 6 months, relative to the model's own normal.
topics.body: An anomaly is the difference from normal: +1 °C means one degree warmer than usual for that month. Seasonal forecasts give tendencies, not daily weather; their skill is highest in the tropics and during strong El Nino years, lowest in mid-latitude winters.

related.title: ENSO sensitivity (how much El Nino reaches a place)

topics.title: Situation briefing (rules vs AI-polished)
topics.short: A plain-English summary of ENSO, the forecast, Koh Samui's level, nearby hazards and data gaps, rebuilt every 6 hours.
topics.body:
An automatic briefing assembled from the tracker's own stored data: the official ENSO status and indices with their dates, the forecast probabilities, the Koh Samui level and its main factors, hazards within 800 km plus major (GDACS orange/red) events worldwide, the 5 latest official bulletins, and which sources are failing or stale. It is rebuilt every 6 hours and immediately when the Koh Samui level changes.

Limits. It summarizes; it does not forecast on its own. If a source is stale or missing, the briefing is only as good as what remains; read the "Data gaps" section. The level "UNKNOWN" means data is insufficient, never "safe".
topics.how_to_read:
- method = rules: every sentence was built by fixed rules from stored values. No AI.
- method = llm: the same facts were rewritten by an AI model (ComputeForge) for readability. The AI is told not to add anything, and its text is thrown away automatically if it contains any number that was not in the rules version.
- `llm_error` explains why the AI version was not used (no key, error, refusal, or a rejected invented number). The rules version is then shown.
- Every section lists its sources with links; dates are UTC.
topics.why_it_matters: It is the fastest way to know "what changed and does it concern us", and it always states what it does not know (missing factors, stale sources) instead of implying all is well.

topics.title: Smoke and dust index (OMPS)
topics.short: Ultraviolet index of smoke and dust, visible even above clouds.
topics.body:
UV aerosol index from the OMPS instrument on NOAA-21.

Limits. Coarse (~50 km); does not give ground-level air quality (see PM2.5 series).
topics.how_to_read: Below 0 to 5 and above: over ~1 = smoke or dust present, over 2-3 = thick smoke.
topics.why_it_matters: El Nino dry seasons bring fire haze from Sumatra and Borneo that can reach the Gulf of Thailand.

topics.title: SOI (Australian Bureau of Meteorology, Troup)
topics.short: Australia's version of the SOI, on a different scale from NOAA's: about 10 times larger. Sustained values below -7 often mean El Nino, above +7 La Nina.
topics.body:
The Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) computes the SOI with the Troup method: the standardised anomaly of the Tahiti minus Darwin pressure difference, multiplied by 10, with a 1933-1992 base period.

So a BoM SOI of -12 is roughly comparable to a NOAA CPC SOI of about -1.2. Do not compare the two numbers directly.

BoM's rule of thumb: sustained values below -7 often indicate El Nino; sustained values above +7 are typical of La Nina.
topics.how_to_read: Negative = El Nino-like. Look at several months: single months are noisy.

sources.title: Australian Bureau of Meteorology -- About the SOI

topics.title: SOI (Southern Oscillation Index, NOAA CPC)
topics.short: The standardised air pressure difference between Tahiti and Darwin. Negative values go with El Nino; positive with La Nina.
topics.body:
The SOI measures the atmosphere half of ENSO. It compares sea-level air pressure at Tahiti (central Pacific) with Darwin (northern Australia).

- During El Nino, pressure rises at Darwin and falls at Tahiti, so Tahiti minus Darwin becomes negative.
- During La Nina, the opposite: positive SOI.

The sign convention is the opposite of the ocean indices: a warm Pacific (positive ONI) goes with a negative SOI. One month of SOI is noisy (a single storm near Darwin or Tahiti can swing it). Look for values that stay negative for several months.

The NOAA CPC version is standardised (in units of standard deviations), so typical values are between about -3 and +3. The Australian version uses a different scale: see SOI (Australian Bureau of Meteorology, Troup).
topics.how_to_read: Below zero for months = consistent with El Nino. In September 2026 the CPC reported both the traditional and equatorial SOI as negative.

sources.title: NOAA CPC -- ENSO frequently asked questions

topics.title: Source and alert filters
topics.short: List only some kinds of sources or states (for example "stale" or "error"), and only some alert levels, kinds or dates.
topics.body:
The sources page can be filtered by category (ocean index, official, maritime, disaster, news, social, local, ...) and by state (ok, stale, empty, error, needs_config, pending). The alert history can be filtered by level, kind and date.

Limits. A source's state reflects its last run only; a source that fails once and then recovers shows ok again. The run history keeps the last 200 runs per source.

- Freshness rules behind "stale": see the help topic source_freshness.
topics.how_to_read: "state = stale,error" is the quick "what is not working right now" view. Alerts are listed newest first.
topics.why_it_matters: When a decision is near, you want to know at a glance which data you can trust and which alerts were already sent.

topics.title: Sources: interval
topics.short: How often the app asks this source for new data. It follows how often the provider really updates, so it does not hammer it for nothing.
topics.body:
Each collector has its own interval: a monthly index is checked every 6-12 hours, disaster alerts every 10-15 minutes, news every 15-60 minutes. A run is also capped at 5 minutes.

The interval is not the age of the data: a source checked every 10 minutes can still serve data that is days old. That is the "Data age" column (Data freshness and the "stale" state).
topics.how_to_read: "every 6 h" = one request every 6 hours. Shorter is not better: most sources update daily or monthly.

related.title: The Sources page and source states

topics.title: Sources: items
topics.short: How many records the last run received: observations, articles, events or status documents.
topics.body: The count of what the last run stored or updated. 0 with the state "empty" means the source answered but had nothing (for example no active cyclone warning, which is good news). A sudden drop to 0 on a source that usually returns many items can mean its format changed; the state then becomes "error" with the reason.
topics.how_to_read: Compare with the usual number for that source, not between sources: an index adds one value a month, a news feed dozens a day.

related.title: The Sources page and source states

topics.title: Sources: last run
topics.short: When the app last contacted the source, the HTTP answer code and how long it took. "Last ok" is the last run that worked.
topics.body:
Every run is logged (the last 200 per source are kept), whether it worked or not, so a silent failure is impossible.

- HTTP 200 = the server answered normally. 4xx = refused or missing (the address changed, or a key is needed); 5xx = the provider's server failed.
- ms = how long the answer took.
- last ok appears when the newest run failed: the data shown comes from that earlier run.
topics.how_to_read: A recent run with HTTP 200 is healthy. A run "2 d ago" on a 1 h interval means the scheduler or the server was stopped.

related.title: The Sources page and source states

topics.title: Sources: success rate
topics.short: Share of the recent runs (up to the last 200) that worked.
topics.body: Below 100 % means the source sometimes fails or times out. The newest good data is still shown with its date. A low rate on a critical Koh Samui source (weather, sea, rain) is worth watching: when it fails for too long, the Samui level turns "Unknown" rather than pretending all is calm.
topics.how_to_read: 95-100 %: reliable. 70-95 %: occasional failures, usually a slow provider. Below 70 %: check the error column and the provider's site.

related.title: The Sources page and source states

topics.title: Space cams -- reading full-disk satellite images
topics.short: Newest Himawari and GOES satellite images: infrared works day and night, true colour only by day.
topics.body:
The newest images from geostationary weather satellites 36,000 km above the equator:
- Himawari-9 (Japan Meteorological Agency) at 140.7 E: the full Earth disk and a Southeast Asia sector covering Thailand and the Gulf of Thailand. New image every 10 minutes.
- GOES-West (GOES-18) over the central / eastern Pacific, where the Nino 3.4 region lies, and GOES-East (GOES-19) over the Americas (Peru / Ecuador).

Limits.

- Pixels are 2-4 km: a single storm cell over Samui is a dot.
- Bright cloud does not always rain; thin high cirrus looks bright in infrared too.
- The image is 10-40 min old when you see it (scan + publish + our check interval).
- For rain now, use the radar layer; for forecasts, the local risk page.
topics.how_to_read:
- Infrared (Himawari B13, GOES band 13): brightness = cold. Bright white blobs are tall, cold thunderstorm tops (heavy rain); grey is low cloud; dark is clear sky or warm sea. Works day and night.
- True colour (Himawari "True Color Reproduction"): what your eye would see; cloud is white, haze and smoke are milky brown-grey. Black at night.
- GeoColor (GOES): true colour in daylight, infrared clouds plus city lights at night.
- A spiral of bright white cloud with a clear centre is a tropical cyclone.
- The time shown is UTC (Koh Samui = UTC + 7).
topics.why_it_matters: El Nino moves the Pacific's big thunderstorm clusters east, away from Indonesia and toward the central Pacific: fewer bright white clusters over the Maritime Continent, more near the date line. On the Southeast Asia sector you can watch storms and squall lines approach the Gulf of Thailand and smoke haze in dry spells.

topics.title: SST anomaly
topics.short: How much warmer (+) or cooler (-) the sea surface is than its 1991-2020 normal for that date, in °C.
topics.body: An SST anomaly is the sea surface temperature minus its normal for that place and date (see Anomaly). Maps of SST anomaly make El Nino easy to see: a long red tongue of warm anomalies along the equator in the eastern Pacific.
topics.how_to_read: Red/orange = warmer than normal, blue = cooler, white or pale = near normal. On the Indices page, values above +0.5 in the Nino regions indicate El Nino-like warmth.

sources.title: NCAR Climate Data Guide -- Nino SST indices

topics.title: Stale data
topics.short: Data older than it should be for that source. Stale values are marked with a clock sign; a stale "all calm" is treated as unknown.
topics.body:
Each source has a maximum age that matches how often it really updates: a few hours for weather forecasts, a day or two for satellite products, about two months for a monthly index.

When the newest data is older than that, it is stale. The value is still shown (with its date and a warning), because it can still be useful context. But for the Samui risk level, a stale factor that would read 0 becomes unknown, and a stale critical factor makes the overall level Unknown.
topics.how_to_read: Look for the "stale" chip and the "as of" date next to every value.

related.title: The Sources page and source states

topics.title: Storm tracks on the map
topics.short: Lines on the map for tropical cyclones: past track and forecast positions from JMA and JTWC.
topics.body:
For JMA and JTWC storms the map item has a line (GeoJSON LineString, [lon, lat]) joining the past track and the forecast positions, and a point at the current position. The payload lists each forecast point with time, winds and distance to Samui.

Limits. Forecast points beyond 72 h are uncertain by several hundred km.
topics.how_to_read: Colour = severity by distance: red within 300 km of Samui, orange within 800 km, green further away. The same storm can appear twice (JMA and JTWC) with slightly different positions and winds.
topics.why_it_matters: A storm's closest forecast approach is what decides whether the sea around Samui will close; watch storms whose line points toward the Gulf of Thailand.

topics.title: Storms / cyclones
topics.short: Days per year with gusts of 75 km/h or more (ERA5 1991-2020). Tropical-cyclone history is added to the note with sources.
topics.body: ERA5 gusts are for a ~30 km cell and underestimate local gusts on exposed coasts and hills. Tropical cyclones are rare events that 30 years of gust statistics do not capture well, so documented landfalls near a place are listed in the note (for Maenam: Typhoon Gay 1989 and Tropical Storm Pabuk 2019). Current cyclones come from GDACS in the place level.
topics.why_it_matters: Storms cut power, block roads and ferries and damage roofs. On an island they can isolate you for days.

thresholds.note: Exposure scale: 0 very low, 1 low, 2 moderate, 3 high, 4 very high. Higher = more exposed. The colour of the matrix cell follows the same scale.

sources.title: GDACS -- Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System

topics.title: TAO/TRITON buoys
topics.short: About 50 moored buoys along the equatorial Pacific that measure sea temperature (surface and deep), air temperature and wind in real time.
topics.body:
The Tropical Atmosphere Ocean (TAO/TRITON) array is a line of buoys anchored across the equatorial Pacific, run by NOAA and Japan's JAMSTEC. They measure the temperature from the surface down to about 500 m, plus winds and air temperature.

They were built after the 1982-83 El Nino, which was not detected in time. They show Kelvin waves and wind bursts as they happen.

The app shows the surface temperature from buoys with a recent reading, on the Map (green dots) and the Indices page.
topics.how_to_read: Warmer readings in the east than usual = El Nino-like. Buoys go offline for maintenance or damage: a missing buoy is not a signal.

topics.title: Teleconnections
topics.short: Links between ENSO in the Pacific and the weather far away. They shift the odds of dry or wet, hot or cool seasons; they are not guarantees.
topics.body:
A teleconnection is a "connection at a distance". When the rain clouds of the tropical Pacific move, they change the air circulation over half of the planet. So a warm Pacific can mean a dry season in Indonesia and Thailand, extra rain in Peru, or a mild winter in Canada.

These links are about probability, not certainty. NOAA notes that the typical El Nino impacts may happen as often as 80 percent of the time in some places, or as rarely as 40 percent in others. A single storm or flood cannot be labelled "an El Nino event": El Nino changes the background odds.
topics.how_to_read: On the map, the dry and wet "impact zones" show where El Nino usually tilts the odds. They are typical patterns, not forecasts for this year.
topics.why_it_matters: Thailand sits in the region that El Nino usually dries out. That is why this app watches water and heat on Samui more closely during an El Nino.

topics.title: The 2026 El Nino
topics.short: NOAA has an El Nino Advisory in force. In September 2026 it gave a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event in late 2026 and early 2027.
topics.body:
What NOAA's Climate Prediction Center said in its 10 September 2026 discussion:

- ENSO Alert System status: El Nino Advisory.
- El Nino strengthened in August, with surface anomalies above +3.0 °C in the eastern equatorial Pacific. Nino 3.4 reached +1.8 °C, Nino 3 +2.5 °C and Nino 1+2 +3.4 °C (Nino 4 only +0.1 °C).
- Subsurface anomalies exceeded +10 °C at depth; the thermocline is deeper than average.
- Rain is enhanced from the central to the eastern Pacific and suppressed over Indonesia.
- For October-December 2026, a 75% chance of a historic event, stronger than any since 1950 (3-month RONI of +2.5 °C or more).
- Overall: more than 90% chance of a very strong event during the northern fall and winter 2026-27.

The 3-month values published by the CPC for June-August 2026: ONI +1.80 °C, RONI +1.36 °C. The app shows the newest values on the Overview and Indices pages.
topics.why_it_matters: A very strong El Nino peaking around the end of 2026 raises the odds of a drier, hotter February-April 2027 on Samui, on top of a water system that was already rationed in August 2026.

topics.title: The Nino regions (1+2, 3, 3.4, 4)
topics.short: Four boxes along the equatorial Pacific where sea temperature is averaged to track ENSO. Nino 3.4 is the main one.
topics.body:
Scientists average the sea surface temperature over fixed boxes of ocean:

- Nino 1+2: off the coast of Peru and Ecuador.
- Nino 3: the eastern equatorial Pacific.
- Nino 3.4: the east-central equatorial Pacific. The reference for El Nino.
- Nino 4: the central and western equatorial Pacific.

The boxes are drawn on the Map page.
topics.how_to_read: When the eastern boxes (1+2, 3) are much warmer than Nino 4, the event is "eastern Pacific" type, like 1997-98 and 2026. When Nino 4 is warmest, it is a "central Pacific" event.
